Genesis 23:1–25:18. Select a Hebrew word for its morphology, lemma, root, senses and the comments anchored to it. A dotted underline marks a word a commentator quotes.

23:1

And Sarah's life was a hundred years and twenty years and seven years: the years of Sarah's life.

and-were lives-of Sarah hundred year and-twenty year and-seven years years-of lives-of Sarah

Grammar
  • וַיִּהְיוּ is a wayyiqtol in the plural, agreeing with חַיֵּי (a plural-form noun), not with the name Sarah. The verb is a copula, so the three sums stand as its predicate.
  • The three sums are in apposition to the life: 'a hundred years', 'twenty years', 'seven years'. Each number is followed by its noun, the singular after the first and second, the plural after the last.
  • The etnaḥta on שָׁנִים divides the verse. Before it are the three sums; after it the summary שְׁנֵי חַיֵּי שָׂרָה, closed by the silluq on the last word.
  • שְׁנֵי חַיֵּי שָׂרָה, 'the years of Sarah's life', is a construct chain that sums up the three numbers. The same closing phrase is used of Abraham (25:7) and Ishmael (25:17).
Commentary (7)
Rashideclines וַיִּהְיוּ֙ חַיֵּ֣י שָׂרָ֔ה מֵאָ֥ה שָׁנָ֛ה וְעֶשְׂרִ֥ים שָׁנָ֖ה וְשֶׁ֣בַע שָׁנִ֑ים
Rashi takes the repeated 'year' to teach that each part is judged alone: a hundred like twenty for sin, twenty like seven for beauty (לְכָךְ נִכְתַּב שָׁנָה בְּכָל כְּלָל וּכְלָל). The English reads the sums as the length of her life; this midrash is not the plain sense.
Hebrew
לְכָךְ נִכְתַּב שָׁנָה בְּכָל כְּלָל וּכְלָל, לוֹמַר לְךָ שֶׁכָּל אֶחָד נִדְרָשׁ לְעַצְמוֹ, בַּת ק' כְּבַת כ' לְחֵטְא, מַה בַּת כ' לֹא חָטְאָה, שֶׁהֲרֵי אֵינָהּ בַּת עֳנָשִׁין, אַף בַּת ק' בְּלֹא חֵטְא, וּבַת כ' כְּבַת ז' לְיֹפִי:
Rashi שְׁנֵ֖י חַיֵּ֥י שָׂרָֽה׃
Hebrew
כֻּלָּן שָׁוִין לְטוֹבָה:
Ibn Ezranormativefollows חַיֵּ֣י
Ibn Ezra: חַיֵּי is a plural form that is not divided (לשון רבים ולא יתפרדו), that is, it has no singular. He adds that the custom of the language is to put the larger number before the smaller, and the reverse also occurs, as in 'the years of Jacob' (שני יעקב). Here the larger number comes first. The English gives the sense 'life' and keeps his order of the numbers.
Hebrew

Rambanfollows מֵאָ֥ה שָׁנָ֛ה וְעֶשְׂרִ֥ים שָׁנָ֖ה
Ramban rejects Rashi's midrash: the midrash rests on the repetition of the word, and 'year, year and years' is the ordinary usage (שָׁנָה שָׁנָה וְשָׁנִים דֶּרֶךְ הַלָּשׁוֹן הוּא). The same form of Ishmael's years does not mean equal goodness. The English reads the sums as plain numbers.

לְשׁוֹן רַשִׁ"י (רש"י על בראשית כ"ג:א'), לְכָךְ נִכְתַּב שָׁנָה בְּכָל כְּלָל וּכְלָל, לוֹמַר לְךָ שֶׁכָּל אֶחָד נִדְרָשׁ לְעַצְמוֹ, בַּת מֵאָה כְּבַת עֶשְׂרִים לְחֵטְא וּבַת עֶשְׂרִים כְּבַת שְׁבַע לְיוֹפִי. וְכֵן כָּתַב בִּשְׁנֵי חַיֵּי אַבְרָהָם (רש"י על בראשית כ"ה:ז'). וְאֵין מִדְרָשׁוֹ זֶה נָכוֹן, שֶׁהֲרֵי בִּשְׁנֵי חַיֵּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל (שם פסוק יז) נֶאֱמַר כִּשְׁנֵי חַיֵּי אַבְרָהָם בְּשָׁוֶה, וְלֹא הָיוּ שָׁוִים בְּטוֹבָה, אֲבָל הָיָה מִתְּחִלָּה רָשָׁע וְעָשָׂה תְּשׁוּבָה בַּסּוֹף. וְעוֹד כִּי שָׁנָה שָׁנָה לְחַלֵּק מַשְׁמַע, וְאֵינֶנּוּ נִדְרָשׁ לְהַשְׁווֹתָן. אֲבָל "שָׁנָה שָׁנָה וְשָׁנִים" דֶּרֶךְ הַלָּשׁוֹן הוּא, וּמָה שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה (בראשית רבה נ"ח:א') בַּת מֵאָה כְּבַת עֶשְׂרִים לְחֵטְא, לֹא דָּרְשׁוּ כֵּן אֶלָּא מִיִּתּוּר הַלָּשׁוֹן שֶׁחָזַר וְאָמַר "שְׁנֵי חַיֵּי שָׂרָה", שֶׁכְּלָלָן וְהִשְׁוָה אוֹתָן. וְלֹא יִדְרְשׁוּ כֵן בְּאַבְרָהָם:
Radakrecords וַיִּהְיוּ֙ חַיֵּ֣י שָׂרָ֔ה מֵאָ֥ה שָׁנָ֛ה
Radak: the text says 'year' and 'years' three times where one would suffice, as it does of Abraham and of Ishmael; some call this an elegance of Hebrew. With the large number it puts the singular 'year' as a general, with the small number the plural 'years' as a particular (דֶּרֶךְ כְּלָל, דֶּרֶךְ פְּרָט). He also mentions the midrash on the sums. The English uses the plural after the last number and the singular after the others, as the Hebrew does.

Hebrew
וַהֲווֹ חַיֵּי שָׂרָה מְאָה וְעֶשְׂרִין וּשְׁבַע שְׁנִין שְׁנֵי חַיֵּי שָׂרָה:
23:2

And Sarah died in Kiriath-arba, that is Hebron, in the land of Canaan; and Abraham came to mourn for Sarah and to weep over her.

and-died Sarah in-Kiriath-arba she Hebron in-land Canaan and-came Abraham to-mourn to-Sarah and-to-weep her

Grammar
  • The etnaḥta on כְּנָעַן ends the first clause, the death and its place. The pashta on וַיָּבֹא opens the second, the coming of Abraham.
  • הִוא חֶבְרוֹן is an identifying clause: the feminine pronoun resumes קִרְיַת אַרְבַּע and says what the place is.
  • לִסְפֹּד לְשָׂרָה וְלִבְכֹּתָהּ: two infinitives with ל, the second with the 3rd fem. suffix and no preposition. Radak notes that this use means 'over her'.
  • וַיָּבֹא is a wayyiqtol, the next event in the narrative. Rashi places Abraham at Beersheba and Ramban has him come from Beersheba; the text does not say (see the commentary).
Commentary (15)
Rashideclines בְּקִרְיַ֥ת אַרְבַּ֛ע
Rashi takes the name as 'four' and says four couples were buried there: Adam and Eve, Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, Jacob and Leah. This is a midrash on the name, and the English does not adopt it.
Hebrew

Rashi וַיָּבֹא֙ אַבְרָהָ֔ם
Hebrew
מִבְּאֵר שֶׁבַע:
Rashideclines לִסְפֹּ֥ד לְשָׂרָ֖ה וְלִבְכֹּתָֽהּ׃
Rashi links Sarah's death to the binding of Isaac: the news of the binding reached her and her soul left her. This is a midrashic cause; the English states no cause.

Ibn Ezranormativefollows אַרְבַּ֛ע
Ibn Ezra: אַרְבַּע is the name of a great man among the giants (שם אדם גדול בענקים). To make him Abraham is a derash, since Abraham was not one of the giants; when Sarah died Abraham was elsewhere, so the text says 'and Abraham came'. The English transliterates the name and does not read it as 'four'. Joshua 14:15 calls Arba 'the greatest man among the Anakim', which agrees with his reading.

Ibn Ezranormativefollows וְלִבְכֹּתָֽהּ׃
Ibn Ezra reads לִבְכֹּתָהּ as 'to weep over her' (לבכות עליה), comparing 'uvkhatah et aviha' (Deuteronomy 21:13). The English keeps this reading: 'to weep over her'.

Rambanrecords וַיָּבֹא֙ אַבְרָהָ֔ם
Ramban holds that Abraham had gone to Beersheba on business that day and came from there on hearing of Sarah's death; he does not hold that Abraham lived there, since Sarah was in Hebron. He notes the Sages' reading 'he came from Mount Moriah' (מֵהַר הַמֹּרִיָּה בָּא). The English does not say where Abraham came from.

"וַיָּשָׁב אַבְרָהָם אֶל נְעָרָיו וַיָּקֻמוּ וַיֵּלְכוּ יַחְדָּו אֶל בְּאֵר שָׁבַע וַיֵּשֶׁב אַבְרָהָם בִּבְאֵר שָׁבַע", לְהוֹרוֹת שֶׁנִּתְעַכֵּב שָׁם וְיָשַׁב בּוֹ שָׁנִים, וְאִם כֵּן לֹא מֵתָה שָׂרָה בְּאוֹתוֹ זְמַן, כִּי לֹא הָיָה אַבְרָהָם דָּר בִּבְאֵר שֶׁבַע וְשָׂרָה דָּרָה בְּחֶבְרוֹן. וְכֵן נִרְאֶה כִּי יִצְחָק נוֹלַד בִּבְאֵר שֶׁבַע, כִּי כָּתוּב תְּחִלָּה (בראשית כ':א') "וַיִּסַּע מִשָּׁם אַבְרָהָם אַרְצָה הַנֶּגֶב וַיֵּשֶׁב בֵּין קָדֵשׁ וּבֵין שׁוּר וַיָּגָר בִּגְרָר", וַאֲבִימֶלֶךְ אָמַר אֵלָיו "הִנֵּה אַרְצִי לְפָנֶיךָ בַּטּוֹב בְּעֵינֶיךָ שֵׁב" (שם טו), וְנִתְיַשֵּׁב שָׁם בָּאָרֶץ הַהִיא בִּבְאֵר שֶׁבַע, שֶׁכֵּן כָּתוּב (בראשית כ"א:כ"ב) "וַיְהִי בָּעֵת הַהִיא וַיֹּאמֶר אֲבִימֶלֶךְ וּפִיכֹל שַׂר צְבָאוֹ אֶל אַבְרָהָם לֵאמֹר", וְאֵין כָּתוּב שֶׁהָלְכוּ אֵלָיו מִגְּרָר וַיִּכְרְתוּ שָׁם הַבְּרִית בִּבְאֵר שֶׁבַע. וְכֵן תִּרְאֶה כִּי הָגָר כַּאֲשֶׁר הוֹצִיאוּ אוֹתָהּ מִבֵּית אַבְרָהָם בְּיוֹם הִגָּמֵל אֶת יִצְחָק הָלְכָה בְּמִדְבַּר בְּאֵר שֶׁבַע (בראשית כ"א:י"ד), שֶׁשָּׁם הָיוּ דָּרִים. אֲבָל אַחַר יָמִים רַבִּים נָסַע מֵאֶרֶץ פְּלִשְׁתִּים וּבָא לְחֶבְרוֹן, וְנִפְטְרָה שָׁם הַצַּדֶּקֶת. אֲבָל לְפִי הַמִּדְרָשׁ צְרִיכִין אָנוּ לוֹמַר כִּי אַבְרָהָם וְשָׂרָה בִּזְמַן הָעֲקֵדָה הָיוּ דָּרִים בְּחֶבְרוֹן, וְשָׁם נִצְטַוָּה, וּמָה שֶׁאָמַר "בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁלִישִׁי וַיִּשָּׂא אַבְרָהָם אֶת עֵינָיו" (בראשית כ"ב:ד'), כִּי לֹא נִגְלָה לוֹ הָהָר חָמַד אֱלֹהִים עַד הַיּוֹם הַשְּׁלִישִׁי, וְהָיָה בִּשְׁנֵי הַיָּמִים הוֹלֵךְ בִּסְבִיבֵי יְרוּשָׁלַיִם וְלֹא הָיָה הָרָצוֹן לְהַרְאוֹת לוֹ. וְאַבְרָהָם אַחַר הָעֲקֵדָה לֹא שָׁב לִמְקוֹמוֹ לְחֶבְרוֹן אֲבָל הָלַךְ תְּחִלָּה אֶל בְּאֵר שֶׁבַע מְקוֹם הָאֶשֶׁל שֶׁלּוֹ, לָתֵת הוֹדָאָה עַל נִסּוֹ, וְשָׁם שָׁמַע בְּמִיתַת שָׂרָה וּבָא. וּמִי שֶׁאָמַר מֵהַר הַמֹּרִיָּה בָּא וּמִי שֶׁאָמַר מִבְּאֵר שֶׁבַע בָּא הַכֹּל טַעַם אֶחָד. וּלְפִי זֶה מַה שֶׁאָמַר הַכָּתוּב "וַיֵּשֶׁב אַבְרָהָם בִּבְאֵר שָׁבַע" (בראשית כ"ב:י"ט) יִהְיֶה עִנְיָנוֹ כִּי בְּשׁוּבוֹ מִן הָעֲקֵדָה שָׁב אֶל בְּאֵר שֶׁבַע, וּמִשָּׁם הָלַךְ לִקְבֹּר אֶת שָׂרָה, וְאַחַר הַקְּבוּרָה מִיָּד חָזַר לִבְאֵר שֶׁבַע וְנִתְיַשֵּׁב שָׁם שָׁנִים. וְהִשְׁלִים הַכָּתוּב עִנְיַן בְּאֵר שֶׁבַע כְּאֶחָד וְאַחֲרֵי כֵן סִפֵּר בַּקְּבוּרָה. וְשָׁם בִּבְאֵר שֶׁבַע נָשָׂא יִצְחָק אֶת רִבְקָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר "וְהוּא יוֹשֵׁב בְּאֶרֶץ הַנֶּגֶב" (בראשית כ"ד:ס"ב). וְזֶה דַּעַת כָּל הַמְּפָרְשִׁים (רש"י והראב"ע והרד"ק), כִּי אַבְרָהָם הָיָה בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר וּבָא מִשָּׁם. וּלְפִי דַּעְתִּי כִּי הָיָה לְשָׂרָה אֹהֶל שָׁם עוֹמֶדֶת וְאַמְהוֹתֶיהָ לְפָנֶיהָ, וְכֵן כָּתוּב (בראשית ל"א:ל"ג) "בְּאֹהֶל יַעֲקֹב וּבְאֹהֶל לֵאָה וּבְאֹהֶל שְׁתֵּי הָאֲמָהֹת", וְהִנֵּה שָׂרָה מֵתָה בָּאֹהֶל אֲשֶׁר לָהּ וְנִכְנַס אַבְרָהָם בָּאֹהֶל עִם אֲחֻזַּת מֵרֵעָיו לִסְפֹּד אוֹתָהּ. אוֹ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לְשׁוֹן "וַיָּבֹא" לֵאמֹר שֶׁנִּתְעוֹרֵר אַבְרָהָם לַהֶסְפֵּד הַזֶּה וְהִתְחִיל לַעֲשׂוֹתוֹ, כִּי כָל מִתְעוֹרֵר וּמַתְחִיל בִּמְלָאכָה יִקָּרֵא בָּא אֵלֶיהָ, וְזֶה לָשׁוֹן מֻרְגָּל בְּדִבְרֵי חֲכָמִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁנִינוּ בְּתָמִיד (פ"ד מ"ג) בָּא לוֹ לַגֵּרָה וְהִנִּיחַ בָּהּ שְׁתֵּי צְלָעוֹת מִכָּאן, בָּא לוֹ לַדֹּפֶן הַשְּׂמָאלִית, בָּא לוֹ לָעֹקֶץ, וְאָמְרָם (בכורות כ) אֲנִי לֹא בָּאתִי לִידֵי הַמִּדָּה הַזּוֹ, וְכֵן בַּכָּתוּב (שמות כב יד) "בָּא בִּשְׂכָרוֹ", שֶׁבָּא "וַיִּשְׁמַע אַבְרָהָם וַיָּבֹא מִמְּקוֹם פְּלוֹנִי":

Ancient Near East
  • Kiriath-arba is the name the text gives to Hebron: Joshua 14:15 says that Hebron was formerly Kiriath-arba. Genesis does not explain the name; the commentators read it as 'four' or as a man's name (see the commentary), and the English keeps it as a name.
23:3

And Abraham rose from before his dead and spoke to the Hittites, saying,

and-rose Abraham from-upon face-of his-dead and-spoke to sons-of Heth saying

Grammar
  • The etnaḥta on מֵתוֹ divides the verse: Abraham rises from before his dead, then he speaks.
  • Two wayyiqtols carry the narrative, with the subject Abraham named once: וַיָּקׇם and וַיְדַבֵּר.
  • מֵעַל פְּנֵי מֵתוֹ is an idiom: 'from before his dead'. The participle used as a noun takes the 3rd masc. suffix, and the text leaves the dead one unnamed here.
  • לֵאמֹר is an infinitive construct with ל. It introduces the speech that begins in 23:4.
Commentary (6)
Ibn Ezranormativefollows פְּנֵ֣י מֵת֑וֹ
Ibn Ezra: מֵתוֹ is a hint to the body (רמז לגוף), so 'his dead' is the corpse itself. The English keeps 'his dead' and names no one.

. רמז לגוף ועוד תמצא פי' לאמר:

Sfornonot-applicable מֵעַ֖ל פְּנֵ֣י מֵת֑וֹ וַיְדַבֵּ֥ר אֶל בְּנֵי חֵ֖ת
Sforno: Abraham was not yet under the full mourning (שֶׁלֹּא חָל עָלָיו אֲבֵלוּת עֲדַיִן), so he could go out and speak. This bears on his status, not on the words.

Ancient Near East
  • The sons of Heth (בְּנֵי־חֵת) are rendered 'the Hittites', as the decisions set. Whether they are the Hittite people of Anatolia, known from the Hittite records, is disputed: some identify the two; others take the sons of Heth to be a group in Canaan, since Genesis 10:15 makes Heth a son of Canaan. The English leaves that question open.
23:4

"I am a sojourner and a resident among you. Give me a possession of a grave among you, that I may bury my dead from before me."

sojourner and-resident I with-you give to-me possession-of grave with-you and-I-will-bury dead-my from-before-me

Grammar
  • גֵּר וְתוֹשָׁב אָנֹכִי is a verbless clause; the English supplies 'I am'.
  • תְּנוּ לִי is imperative plural, addressed to the Hittites of 23:3, with the dative suffix on לִי.
  • אֲחֻזַּת קֶבֶר is a construct chain: 'possession of a grave'. The request is for a burial holding, a possession of ground for a grave.
  • The etnaḥta on עִמָּכֶם divides the first clause from the second. וְאֶקְבְּרָה is a cohortative following the imperative; it states the purpose of the request.

The speech opens here and closes at the end of the verse.

Commentary (10)
Rashideclines גֵּר וְתוֹשָׁ֥ב אָנֹכִ֖י עִמָּכֶ֑ם
Rashi glosses גֵּר as one from another land (גֵּר מֵאֶרֶץ אַחֶרֶת) who has settled among them. Then, as a homily: if you wish, I am a ger; if not, I will be a toshav and take it by right (וְאֶטְּלֶנָּה מִן הַדִּין), for the Holy One said to my seed 'I will give this land'. The English keeps the plain status; the homily is not the plain sense.

Ibn Ezra glosses גֵּר as the one who lodges by himself (לבדו הוא הלן). The English 'sojourner' keeps that sense.

Abraham says 'I am a resident among you' because death is decreed for us, and he has no holding like an inheritance (נחלה) in the land, nor a place bought for money to bury a dead man. Ancient Near East
  • גֵּר וְתוֹשָׁב together describe a resident outsider who holds no land of his own among the people he lives with. How the two words differ is a matter of the commentators' readings (see the commentary). The burial ground asked for is a plot of ground, which is why Abraham asks for a holding and the Hittites, in 23:6, answer in terms of their graves.
23:5

And the Hittites answered Abraham, saying to him,

and-answered sons-of Heth (object) Abraham saying to-him

Grammar
  • The tevir on חֵת divides the subject from the rest of the verse. The tipḥa on אַבְרָהָם and the silluq on לוֹ end the clause.
  • וַיַּעֲנוּ is a wayyiqtol, 3rd masc. plural, and its subject 'the sons of Heth' comes after it.
  • לֵאמֹר לוֹ introduces a speech; the speech follows in 23:6 and opens there.
Commentary (2)
Radakrecords וַיַּעֲנ֧וּ
Radak: they agreed among themselves before they answered (הִסְכִּימוּ בֵּינֵיהֶם), and said this to him. The English keeps 'answered' and does not add the agreement.
Hebrew
הִסְכִּימוּ בֵּינֵיהֶם שֶׁיַּעֲנוּהוּ וְיֹאמְרוּ לוֹ זֶה.

Hebrew

23:6

"Hear us, my lord; you are a prince of God among us. In the choicest of our graves bury your dead. No man of us will withhold his grave from you, from burying your dead."

hear-us my-lord prince of God you among-us in-choicest-of graves-of-us bury (object) your-dead man of-us (object) his-grave not will-withhold from-you from-burying your-dead

Grammar
  • שְׁמָעֵנוּ אֲדֹנִי: the plural suffix 'us' with the singular 'my lord'. The speakers are many, the form of address is to one man (Radak).
  • נְשִׂיא אֱלֹהִים אַתָּה בְּתוֹכֵנוּ has no verb: אַתָּה is the subject and נְשִׂיא אֱלֹהִים the predicate; the English supplies 'are'.
  • בְּמִבְחַר קְבָרֵינוּ קְבֹר: the locative phrase 'in the choicest of our graves' comes before the imperative 'bury'.
  • לֹא־יִכְלֶה מִמְּךָ מִקְּבֹר: a negated yiqtol; 'his grave' comes first as object. The first מִ is 'from you' (a verb of withholding takes מִן of the one denied); the second, with the infinitive, gives what is withheld: 'from burying'.
  • The silluq on מֵתֶךָ ends the speech; the tipḥa on מִמְּךָ is a lesser stop inside the last clause.

The speech runs from 23:6 to the end of the verse.

Ancient Near East
  • נָשִׂיא, 'prince', is the title of the head of a tribe or clan in the text. The Hittites give it to Abraham, who is a stranger among them (23:4).
  • נְשִׂיא אֱלֹהִים is read in two ways. 'A prince of God' takes אֱלֹהִים as the possessor, a man raised up by God (Ibn Ezra relates it to Abraham as a prophet). Others take אֱלֹהִים as an intensifier, as in 'cedars of God' or 'mountains of God' (Psalm 80:11, 36:7), and render 'a mighty prince'. Both are readings of the words; the English keeps the first, with Ibn Ezra.
23:7

And Abraham rose and bowed down to the people of the land, to the Hittites.

and-rose Abraham and-bowed-down to-people-of the-land to-sons-of Heth

Grammar
  • וַיָּקׇם וַיִּשְׁתַּחוּ: two wayyiqtols in sequence, the second a hithpalel of שָׁחָה (BDB; others analyse it as a hishtaphel).
  • לְעַם הָאָרֶץ לִבְנֵי חֵת: two datives. The tipḥa on הָאָרֶץ divides them, and the silluq on חֵת ends the verse.
  • The darga on וַיָּקׇם and the merkha on וַיִּשְׁתַּחוּ mark the two verbs; the verse is one short narrative sentence.
Commentary (4)
Ibn Ezranormativefollows the whole verse
Ibn Ezra: the hishtahawah is the bowing of the head a man makes to honour another (שישוח ראשו), and Moses bowed to his father-in-law too. Those who say the bowing was for the sake of the Name (worship) have said nothing, since the text says he bowed to the Hittites. The English has no object of worship.
Hebrew

  • עַם הָאָרֶץ, 'the people of the land', is here the citizens of the town who act for it; the phrase is used with other senses in later books. The text gives it as a second name for the sons of Heth, and Sforno reads it as their leading men.
23:8

And he spoke with them, saying, "If it is your will to bury my dead from before me, hear me, and entreat for me with Ephron son of Zohar,

and-spoke with-them saying if there-is with your-soul to-bury (object) my-dead from-before-me hear-me and-entreat for-me in-Ephron son-of Zohar

Grammar
  • אִם־יֵשׁ אֶת־נַפְשְׁכֶם is a conditional whose idiom means 'if you are willing'. The English 'If it is your will' gives that sense.
  • לִקְבֹּר אֶת־מֵתִי מִלְּפָנַי is the infinitive that states what the will is. 'My dead' is its object.
  • שְׁמָעוּנִי וּפִגְעוּ־לִי: two plural imperatives, addressed to the men of the city (the sons of Heth), form the apodosis of the condition.
  • The speech runs on into 23:9, which is outside this unit.

The quotation is left open: the speech closes in 23:9, which is outside this unit.

Rashi נַפְשְׁכֶ֗ם

רְצוֹנְכֶם:

23:9

that he may give me the cave of Machpelah, which is his, which is at the end of his field; for full silver let him give it to me among you as a possession of a grave."

and-let-him-give to-me [object] the-cave-of the-Machpelah which to-him which at-end-of his-field for-silver full let-him-give-it to-me in-midst-of-you for-possession-of grave

Grammar
  • וְיִתֶּן לִי (23:9.1–2) is a jussive after ו: 'that he may give me'. The clause carries on Abraham's speech, which began in 23:8.
  • The two relatives אֲשֶׁר־לוֹ and אֲשֶׁר בִּקְצֵה שָׂדֵהוּ both describe the cave: 'which is his, which is at the end of his field'. The field is named as the cave's location.
  • בְּכֶסֶף מָלֵא: the ב is the price, 'for full silver'. The verb יִתְּנֶנָּה (23:9.13) repeats the request; its feminine suffix refers back to מְעָרָה, the cave.
  • The etnaḥta on שָׂדֵהוּ (23:9.10) divides the verse. לַאֲחֻזַּת קָבֶר, a noun phrase, ends it with the silluq on קָבֶר (23:9.17).

Abraham's speech opens in 23:8, in the previous unit, and closes at the end of this verse; the closing quotation mark is here. The Hebrew asks for the cave: Radak: Abraham asked only for the cave, not the field. The verb is 'give', not 'sell' (see Ramban). 'Full silver' is silver with nothing short (Ibn Ezra).

  • The price is stated as a weight of silver, without a coin or a unit of currency. Coined money came much later than the time of this story; the silver was weighed out (see 23:16).

23:10

Now Ephron was dwelling among the Hittites, and Ephron the Hittite answered Abraham in the hearing of the Hittites, to all who came in at the gate of his city, saying,

and-Ephron sitting in-midst-of sons-of Heth and-answered Ephron the-Hittite [object] Abraham in-ears-of sons-of Heth to-all comers-of gate-of his-city saying

Grammar
  • וְעֶפְרוֹן יֹשֵׁב (23:10.1–2) is a clause of situation: the participle gives the setting of Ephron when Abraham spoke.
  • וַיַּעַן עֶפְרוֹן הַחִתִּי אֶת־אַבְרָהָם (23:10.6–10) is a wayyiqtol. The subject comes after the verb, and the English puts it first.
  • בְּאׇזְנֵי בְנֵי־חֵת (23:10.11–13) names the audience as the same people as 23:10.4–5: the Hittites are the witnesses.
  • לְכֹל בָּאֵי שַׁעַר עִירוֹ (23:10.14–17) is a construct chain: 'to all of those coming in at the gate of his city'. The gate is where the men of the town were gathered.
  • The etnaḥta on חֵת (23:10.5) divides the verse; the silluq on לֵאמֹר (23:10.18) ends it.

The quotation opens in 23:11, the first verse of Ephron's speech, so this verse ends with 'saying' and no quotation mark. The decision renders בְּנֵי־חֵת as 'the Hittites'; its relation to the Hittites of Anatolia is disputed (see the context). Rashi's remarks on this verse are midrash and are not followed.

A midrash on Ephron's standing, not the plain sense of יָשַׁב; the English reads 'was dwelling'.

Ancient Near East
  • בְּנֵי־חֵת, 'the sons of Heth', is the Hebrew name for the people here. Whether they were Hittites of Anatolia, or a Canaanite group named after Heth, son of Canaan (Genesis 10:15), is disputed. The English stays neutral, rendering 'the Hittites' as the decision requires.
  • The city gate was the public place where business was done before the men of the town. A land transaction made at the gate before the elders and witnesses is described in Ruth 4:1–11.
Apparatus
  • Rashi notes a defective spelling (כְּתִיב חָסֵר) in this verse without naming a word. The pack gives no variant, and the English is unaffected.
23:11

"No, my lord, hear me. The field I have given to you, and the cave which is in it I have given to you; in the sight of my people I have given it to you. Bury your dead."

no my-lord hear-me the-field I-have-given to-you and-the-cave which in-it to-you I-have-given-it in-eyes-of sons-of my-people I-have-given-it to-you bury dead-of-you

Grammar
  • לֹא אֲדֹנִי שְׁמָעֵנִי: the negative stands before the vocative. The imperative שְׁמָעֵנִי has the first person suffix: 'hear me'.
  • The three qatals נָתַתִּי (23:11.5, 23:11.11, 23:11.15) are completed acts within the speech, rendered 'I have given'.
  • The second person suffix is written ךְ in לָךְ (23:11.6) and לָּךְ (23:11.16), the pausal form of masculine ךָ, as in לְךָ (23:11.10). All three address Abraham, and the English 'you' serves.
  • וְהַמְּעָרָה אֲשֶׁר־בּוֹ: the relative clause's 'in it' is the field, so the cave is the one in the field.
  • The imperative קְבֹר מֵתֶךָ (23:11.17–18) ends the speech: 'bury your dead'. The etnaḥta on נְתַתִּיהָ (23:11.11) divides it, and the silluq on מֵתֶךָ ends the verse.

Ephron's speech. Its opening and closing quotation marks are both in this verse. Whether the 'no' refuses the price (Rashi, Radak) or Ibn Ezra's gloss (כֵּן, 'yes, my lord, only hear me': a courtesy against the word) is right is not decided by the English, which keeps the word 'No'. Whether the field and cave are a gift (Radak) is left to 23:15, where a price is named.

Grammar
  • וַיִּשְׁתַּחוּ is a hitpaʿel wayyiqtol: 'and he bowed down'. The verse is one sequential clause.
  • לִפְנֵי: 'before', from פְּנֵי, the construct plural of פָּנֶה; the prepositional phrase gives the place of the bow.
  • עַם הָאָרֶץ: a fixed phrase for the men of the land, here the Hittites of 23:7 and 23:10. It is used again in 23:13, where Abraham speaks in their hearing.
  • The zaqef qaton on אַבְרָהָם (23:12.2) divides the verse; the silluq on הָאָרֶץ (23:12.5) ends it.

The Hebrew names the people, not the one bowed to. Ibn Ezra takes the bow to be before the people, given to Ephron as praise; Radak takes it to be to Ephron. The English keeps the words.

Ibn Ezranormativefollows לִפְנֵ֖י עַ֥ם הָאָֽרֶץ׃

Ancient Near East
  • A bow to the ground before a person or a group of standing was a sign of respect. Compare 33:3, where Jacob bows seven times before Esau.
  • עַם הָאָרֶץ, 'the people of the land', here means the local landholding citizens, the same men the text calls 'the Hittites' (23:7, 23:10). In later books the phrase has other senses, and its meaning there is debated.
23:13

And he spoke to Ephron in the hearing of the people of the land, saying, "But if you would hear me, I give the price of the field; take from me, and I will bury my dead there."

and-he-spoke to-Ephron in-ears-of people-of the-land saying but if you if-only hear-me I-have-given the-silver of-the-field take from-me and-I-bury [object] my-dead there

Grammar
  • וַיְדַבֵּר ... לֵאמֹר: the speech introduction. The quotation opens here, at the start of Abraham's speech.
  • אַךְ אִם ... לוּ שְׁמָעֵנִי: 'but if you would hear me'. The particle אַךְ restricts the condition, and לוּ with the imperative makes it a wish.
  • נָתַתִּי כֶּסֶף הַשָּׂדֶה: the qatal is performative, 'I give the price of the field'. Rashi reads 'ready with me'.
  • קַח מִמֶּנִּי: the imperative with מִן, 'take from me'. The object, the silver, is understood from the clause before.
  • וְאֶקְבְּרָה: a cohortative after ו, 'and I will bury'; the burial is the result of taking the price.

The English 'I give' takes the qatal as performative, as Radak does ('from now I will give'). Ibn Ezra's second reading, that the silver is already given, is recorded in the commentary. 'Take from me' carries no object: the Hebrew names none in the verb.

Grammar
  • וַיַּעַן עֶפְרוֹן אֶת־אַבְרָהָם: the reply is a wayyiqtol with the subject after the verb and the object marker before Abraham.
  • לֵאמֹר לוֹ is the formula that introduces speech: 'saying to him'. The speech follows in 23:15.
  • The tevir on עֶפְרוֹן (23:14.2) and the tipḥa on אַבְרָהָם (23:14.4) mark pauses within the verse; the silluq on לוֹ ends it.

The quotation opens at the start of 23:15, so this verse ends with the introduction and no quotation mark.

"My lord, hear me. Land, four hundred shekels of silver, between me and you: what is it? And bury your dead."

Grammar
  • אֶרֶץ אַרְבַּע מֵאֹת שֶׁקֶל־כֶּסֶף is a noun phrase with no verb: 'land, four hundred shekels of silver'. The English adds no verb.
  • בֵּינִי וּבֵינְךָ מַה־הִוא: 'between me and you, what is it?' The question asks what the land is, between the two of them, in silver.
  • וְאֶת־מֵתְךָ קְבֹֽר: an imperative after the question, 'and bury your dead'.
  • The etnaḥta on הִוא (23:15.11) divides the speech; the silluq on קְבֹֽר (23:15.14) ends it.

The price is a noun phrase, and the English keeps it so. The question 'what is it?' is read by Rashi and Sforno as 'it is a trifle' and by Radak as 'it makes no difference'; the English keeps the question, and the readings are recorded. Ephron's speech opens and closes here.

23:16

And Abraham listened to Ephron, and Abraham weighed out to Ephron the silver which he had spoken in the hearing of the Hittites, four hundred shekels of silver by the merchants' standard.

and-listened Abraham to Ephron and-weighed Abraham to-Ephron [object] the-silver which spoke in-ears-of sons-of Heth four-hundred shekels silver passing to-the-trader

Grammar
  • וַיִּשְׁקֹל ... אֶת־הַכֶּסֶף: 'weighed out' with the silver as object. The price is weighed, not counted.
  • The silver is named twice: 'the silver which he had spoken' and 'four hundred shekels of silver'. The second names the amount.
  • אֲשֶׁר דִּבֶּר בְּאׇזְנֵי בְנֵי־חֵת: the relative clause in the qatal: the amount was named in the hearing of the Hittites (23:10, 23:15).
  • עֹבֵר לַסֹּחֵר: the participle of עָבַר, 'passing', with לְ and a participle used as a noun, 'the merchant': silver current by the merchants' standard.
  • The etnaḥta on חֵת (23:16.14) divides the verse; the silluq on לַסֹּחֵר (23:16.20) ends it.

The English 'by the merchants' standard' gives עֹבֵר לַסֹּחֵר: silver as current among merchants, weighed by their standard. Ibn Ezra reads 'chosen silver', and Radak 'full weight, as merchants are exact'; both are about the quality of the weighed silver, which the English carries. The weighing of silver before coined money is in the context.

Commentary (6)
Rashirecords וַיִּשְׁקֹ֤ל אַבְרָהָם֙ לְעֶפְרֹ֔ן
Rashi: the name is written without a vav (עפרן), because Ephron said much and did not do even a little (Bava Metzia 87): he took from him large shekels, kantars, as 'current with the merchant' (accepted by weight everywhere; Bekhorot 50), for in some places the shekels are large, kantars (centenaria in French). The English keeps 'shekels'; the reading is recorded.
Hebrew
חָסֵר וָי"ו; לְפִי שֶׁאָמַר הַרְבֵּה, וַאֲפִלּוּ מְעַט לֹא עָשָׂה (בבא מציעא פ"ז), שֶׁנָּטַל מִמֶּנוּ שְׁקָלִים גְּדוֹלִים שֶׁהֵן קַנְטָרִין, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר עֹבֵר לַסֹּחֵר, שֶׁמִּתְקַבְּלִים בְּשֶׁקֶל בְּכָל מָקוֹם (שם ובכורות נ'), וְיֵשׁ מָקוֹם שֶׁשִּׁקְלֵיהֶן גְּדוֹלִים, שֶׁהֵן קַנְטָרִין צנטינא"רש בלע"ז:
Ibn Ezranormativefollows עֹבֵ֖ר לַסֹּחֵֽר׃
Ibn Ezra: he would take only chosen silver (שֶׁלֹּא יִקַּח כִּי אִם כֶּסֶף נִבְחָר). The English 'by the merchants' standard' names the standard of the silver, which is the quality the commentary names.
Hebrew
שלא יקח כי אם כסף נבחר:
Radakfollows עֹבֵ֖ר לַסֹּחֵֽר׃
Radak: 'silver full by weight, as the merchants carry and pay with it, for they are exact about the weight of silver'. The English 'by the merchants' standard' agrees.
Hebrew
כֶּסֶף מָלֵא בְּמִשְׁקָלוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנּוֹשְׂאִים וְנוֹתְנִים בּוֹ הַסּוֹחֲרִים, כִּי הֵם מְדַקְדְּקִים בְּמִשְׁקַל הַכֶּסֶף.
Targum Onkelosfollows the whole verse
Onkelos: 'and Abraham accepted from Ephron', renders וַיִּשְׁמַע as 'accepted', and the silver as 'shekels of silver accepted as merchandise in every province' (מִתְקַבֵּל סְחוֹרָא בְּכָל מְדִינְתָּא). The English follows his sense of silver accepted by the merchants' standard; 'listened to' keeps the Hebrew verb.
Hebrew
וְקַבֵּל אַבְרָהָם מִן עֶפְרוֹן וּתְקַל אַבְרָהָם לְעֶפְרוֹן יָת כַּסְפָּא דְּמַלֵּיל קֳדָם בְּנֵי חִתָּאָה אַרְבַּע מְאָה סִלְעִין דִּכְסַף מִתְקַבֵּל סְחוֹרָא (נ"י דְּמִתְקַבֵּל סְחוֹרָתָא) בְּכָל מְדִינְתָּא:
Sfornorecords וַיִּשְׁמַ֣ע אַבְרָהָם֮ עֶפְרוֹן֒
Sforno: Abraham agreed to Ephron's view of the field's value (הִסְכִּים לְדַעְתּוֹ בְּעֵרֶךְ הַשָּׂדֶה). The English keeps 'listened to'; the agreement is recorded.
Hebrew
הִסְכִּים לְדַעְתּוֹ בְּעֵרֶךְ הַשָּׂדֶה.
Sfornofollows וַיִּשְׁקֹ֤ל
Sforno: וַיִּשְׁקֹל means 'paid', as in 'a talent of silver you shall weigh' (1 Kings 20:39). The English 'weighed out' keeps the payment by weight.
Hebrew
פָּרַע כְּמוֹ "אוֹ כִּכַּר כֶּסֶף תִּשְׁקוֹל" (מלכים א כ:לט).
Ancient Near East
  • Before coined money, silver was paid by weight: it was weighed on a balance, and the shekel was first a unit of weight. Coins came much later, so the 'money' of this passage is weighed silver.
  • The silver is named in the hearing of the Hittites and weighed in their presence, so that the transfer is witnessed (compare 23:17–18 for the record of the sale).
Apparatus
  • Rashi remarks on a missing vav in this phrase (חָסֵר וָי״ו) and draws a lesson from it. The defective spelling of the name, לְעֶפְרֹן (23:16.7), is the same name; the English is unaffected.
23:17

And the field of Ephron which was in Machpelah, which was before Mamre, was made over: the field and the cave which was in it, and all the trees which were in the field, which were within its whole border all around.

and-stood field-of Ephron which in-the-Machpelah which before Mamre the-field and-the-cave which in-it and-all-of the-tree which in-the-field which in-all-of its-border round-about

Grammar
  • The verse is a chain of nouns, each with an אֲשֶׁר clause that attaches it to the nearest place or thing: 'in Machpelah', 'before Mamre', 'in it', 'in the field', 'within its border'. The English uses 'which' for each.
  • The verb וַיָּקָם is a wayyiqtol, third person masculine singular: it continues the narrative in the past, and its subject follows it. It agrees with the first noun, שְׂדֵה עֶפְרוֹן, 'the field of Ephron', and the rest of the verse spells out what the field comprises.
  • הַשָּׂדֶה in 23:17.9 repeats the field, now with the article, in apposition: the field, and the cave and the trees that are in it and within its border.
  • Accents: the etnaḥta on מַמְרֵא (23:17.8) divides the verse, after the place names; the silluq on סָבִיב (23:17.20) ends it.

The English puts the verb after the place names, as the sense of the whole sentence requires. The Hebrew gives no preposition for the buyer in this verse; 'to Abraham' comes in 23:18, and the English adds nothing here.

Commentary (6)
Rashifollows וַיָּ֣קׇם שְׂדֵ֣ה עֶפְר֗וֹן
Rashi says the field's standing (תְּקוּמָה) was that it passed from a commoner's hand to a king's, which is a midrashic remark; his plain sense is that the field, the cave and the trees stand for Abraham as a purchase. The English follows the plain sense (the sale stood good) and not the king.
Hebrew
תְּקוּמָה הָיְתָה לוֹ, שֶׁיָּצָא מִיַּד הֶדְיוֹט לְיַד מֶלֶךְ; וּפְשׁוּטוֹ שֶׁל מִקְרָא וַיָּקָם הַשָּׂדֶה וְהַמְּעָרָה אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ וְכָל הָעֵץ לְאַבְרָהָם לְמִקְנָה וגו':
Ibn Ezranormativefollows וַיָּ֣קׇם
Ibn Ezra: 'נתקיים ועמד השדה למקנה', the field was confirmed and stood as a purchase. He says this verse is joined (דבק) to the verse above it, likewise 'גר ותושב אנכי' (23:4), and that the ten that the Gaon mentioned are not joined. The comment ends at 'וטעם:' in the source edition itself. The English takes קום as 'stood' in the sense of standing good.
Hebrew
נתקיים ועמד השדה למקנה, והנה זה הפסוק דבק עם הפסוק שהוא למעלה וכן "גר ותושב אנכי" (בראשית כג ד) והעשרה שהזכיר הגאון אינם דבקים, וטעם:
Radakfollows וַיָּ֣קׇם
Radak: it stood for Abraham as a purchase, like 'and it shall stand to him' (Lev 27:19 as he cites it), that is, it was confirmed in his hand. This supports 'stood' as standing good.
Hebrew
קָם לְאַבְרָהָם לְמִקְנָה, וְכֵן ״וְקָם לוֹ״ (ויקרא כז:יט), כְּלוֹמַר נִתְקַיֵּם בְּיָדוֹ.
Radakrecords אֲשֶׁר֙ לִפְנֵ֣י מַמְרֵ֑א
Radak: the field and the cave lay before the city, and the city is called Mamre and is also called Hebron, as in 'on the face of Mamre, that is Hebron' (23:19). The English keeps 'before Mamre' and names Hebron in 23:19.
Hebrew
הַשָּׂדֶה וְהַמְּעָרָה הָיוּ לִפְנֵי הָעִיר, וְהָעִיר נִקְרֵאת מַמְרֵא וְנִקְרֵאת חֶבְרוֹן כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב ״עַל פְּנֵי מַמְרֵא הִיא חֶבְרוֹן״ (בראשית כג:יט).
Targum Onkelosfollows the whole verse
Targum Onkelos renders the verb as וְקָם, 'stood', and the field as חֲקַל, 'field', and keeps the cave and the trees. It agrees with the English.
Hebrew
וְקָם חֲקַל עֶפְרוֹן דִּי בְּכָפֶלְתָּא דִּי קֳדָם מַמְרֵא חַקְלָא וּמְעַרְתָּא דִּי בֵיהּ וְכָל אִילָנֵי דִּי בְחַקְלָא דִּי בְכָל תְּחוּמֵיהּ סְחוֹר סְחוֹר:
Sfornorecords וַיָּ֣קׇם שְׂדֵ֣ה
Sforno: the field was confirmed by the seals of the deed of purchase (נִתְקַיֵּם בְּחוֹתָמָיו שֶׁל סֵפֶר הַמִּקְנָה). This says how it was confirmed, an account of what happened; the English keeps 'stood' and does not name the seals.
Hebrew
נִתְקַיֵּם בְּחוֹתָמָיו שֶׁל סֵפֶר הַמִּקְנָה.
Ancient Near East
  • The field is conveyed with its cave and with the trees within its borders, so the whole plot is named, not the field alone. The text describes it by its border on all sides.
Apparatus
  • The sense 'stood good' (a legal sense) is the reading taken. The Hebrew of the verse does not say how it was confirmed; Sforno's seals and Radak's 'in his hand' are readings of that, not of the words.
23:18

to Abraham as a purchase, in the sight of the Hittites, among all who came in at the gate of his city.

to-Abraham to-purchase to-eyes-of sons-of Heth in-all-of those-coming-in-of gate-of city-his

Grammar
  • The verse has no finite verb. It is a set of prepositional phrases that go with the verb 'stood' of 23:17: to Abraham, as a purchase, in the sight of the Hittites, among the people at the gate.
  • בָּאֵי שַׁעַר עִירוֹ is a participle in the construct: 'those coming in' (of) the gate of his city. The clause names the people who went through the gate, the public of the city.
  • לְעֵינֵי is a dual construct form ('the eyes of'), used as a fixed phrase meaning 'in the sight of'.
  • Accents: the etnaḥta on חֵת (23:18.5) divides the verse into two halves, 'to Abraham as a purchase, in the sight of the sons of Heth' and 'among all who came in at the gate of his city'. The tipḥa on לְמִקְנָה and on בְּכֹל are lesser disjunctives; the merkha on לְאַבְרָהָם and the munaḥ on לְעֵינֵי are conjunctive; the silluq on עִירוֹ ends the verse.

The verse is a fragment with no verb. The English keeps it as a fragment; the sense of the verb comes from 23:17.

Commentary (7)
Rashifollows בְּכֹ֖ל בָּאֵ֥י שַֽׁעַר עִירֽוֹ׃
Rashi reads בְּכֹל as 'in the midst of all of them, and in the presence of all of them he transferred it to him' (בְּקֶרֶב כֻּלָּם וּבְמַעֲמַד כֻּלָּם הִקְנָהוּ לוֹ). The English takes the preposition as 'among' in his first sense.
Hebrew
בְּקֶרֶב כֻּלָּם וּבְמַעֲמַד כֻּלָּם הִקְנָהוּ לוֹ:
Ibn Ezranormativefollows לְעֵינֵ֣י בְנֵי חֵ֑ת
Ibn Ezra: 'in the sight of the sons of Heth' means 'the men of the place' (את אנשי המקום). The sons of Heth are the local population. The comment ends at 'וטעם:' in the source edition itself, so no reason is given there. The English keeps 'the Hittites' (the decisions) as the name of that group.
Hebrew
את אנשי המקום, וטעם:
Ibn Ezranormativefollows the whole verse
Ibn Ezra, normative: 'all who came in at the gate of his city' means 'every one who passes and returns' (כָּל עוֹבֵר וָשָׁב). The phrase is everyone who went through the gate. The English keeps 'came in at the gate' and adopts his reading of who the group is.
Hebrew
כל עובר ושב:
Radakrecords לְעֵינֵ֣י בְנֵי חֵ֑ת
Radak: Abraham weighed the silver before them, Ephron sold to him before them, and the deed of purchase was made. He takes the witnesses to be present at the weighing and the sale. That is an account of what happened, so it stays in the note; the English keeps the words.
Hebrew
לְעֵינֵיהֶם שָׁקַל הַכֶּסֶף לְעֶפְרוֹן, וּלְעֵינֵיהֶם מָכַר לוֹ עֶפְרוֹן, וְעָשָׂה לוֹ סֵפֶר מִקְנָה.
Radakfollows the whole verse
Radak: all who came in at the gate of his city, who were there at the time of the purchase. He takes the group as the people present as witnesses, which the English keeps.
Hebrew
עִם כָּל בָּאֵי שַׁעַר עִירוֹ שֶׁהָיוּ שָׁם בְּעֵת הַמִּקְנָה. וְקַדְמָאָה לְכֹל וּבַתְרָאָה
Radaknot-applicable בְּכֹ֖ל
Radak gives a masoretic note on the spelling בְּכֹל: one verse is its sign (וְחַד פֶּסֶק סִימָן, 'one verse is the sign'), Exodus 27:19, 'לְכֹל כְּלֵי הַמִּשְׁכָּן בְּכָל עֲבֹדָתוֹ'. It concerns the spelling and does not bear on the sense.
Hebrew
, וְחַד פֶּסֶק סִימָן ״לְכֹל כְּלֵי הַמִּשְׁכָּן בְּכָל עֲבֹדָתוֹ״ (שמות כז:יט).
Targum Onkelosfollows the whole verse
Targum Onkelos renders למקנה as לִזְבִינוֹהִי, 'as his purchase' (a noun with a suffix), which agrees with 'purchase'. He renders בְּנֵי־חֵת as בְּנֵי חִתָּאָה, and בָּאֵי שַׁעַר as עָלֵי תְּרַע, 'those who enter the gate'. The English 'came in at the gate' agrees.
Hebrew
לְאַבְרָהָם לִזְבִינוֹהִי לְעֵינֵי בְּנֵי חִתָּאָה בְּכָל עָלֵי תְּרַע קַרְתֵּיהּ:
Ancient Near East
  • בְּנֵי־חֵת, 'the sons of Heth', is rendered 'the Hittites' as the decisions require. Whether this people is connected with the Hittites of Anatolia (Hatti) is disputed. Some take the name as the same as that of the Anatolian Hittites, who had a kingdom in Anatolia in the second millennium BCE; others note that the names in this chapter (Ephron, Zohar) are West Semitic and the setting is the hill country of Canaan, and take them as a local people of Canaan. Ramban holds that the Hittites were of the families of Canaan, as he says on 23:19. The English does not decide the question.
  • The city gate was the usual place for public business in the ancient Near East, and dealings there were witnessed by the people present. The verse names that public as the witnesses of the sale.
23:19

And afterwards Abraham buried Sarah, his wife, in the cave of the field of Machpelah, before Mamre, that is Hebron, in the land of Canaan.

and-after that buried Abraham [object] Sarah his-wife to the-cave-of field-of the-Machpelah upon face-of Mamre she Hebron in-land-of Canaan

Grammar
  • The phrase ואחרי כן is an idiom, 'after that'. It links this sentence to the purchase of 23:17 and 23:18.
  • The verb is a qatal after a fronted time phrase, so it is past. The verb comes first, then the subject Abraham, then the object Sarah, marked with אֶת.
  • The pronoun הִוא (23:19.15) is the Pentateuch's spelling הוא for the feminine, read הִיא (qere). It is feminine, 'she, it', and works as the copula: the place called Mamre, it is Hebron. In 23:2 the same city is 'Kiriath-arba, that is Hebron'.
  • The construct chain מְעָרַת שְׂדֵה הַמַּכְפֵּלָה is 'the cave of the field of Machpelah', with the article on the last noun.
  • Accents: tevir on הַמַּכְפֵּלָה (23:19.11) and etnaḥta on חֶבְרוֹן (23:19.16) divide the verse; the silluq on כְּנָעַן (23:19.18) ends it.

The English reads the verb in the past and keeps the Hebrew order of the place phrases. 'Into' keeps the preposition's sense of motion; see the token note.

Commentary (5)
Ibn Ezranormativefollows וְאַחֲרֵי כֵן֩ קָבַ֨ר אַבְרָהָ֜ם אֶת שָׂרָ֣ה
Ibn Ezra, normative: 'and from then the field stood as a burial holding for him and his seed' (ומאז נתקיים השדה לאחוזת קבר לו ולזרעו). The passage is told, he says, to make known the excellence of the land of Israel over all lands, for the living and the dead, and to fulfil God's word to Abraham that he should have a possession. The English 'afterwards' is consistent with this; the purposes he gives are homily and are not in the English.
Hebrew
ומאז נתקיים השדה לאחוזת קבר לו ולזרעו ונזכרה זאת הפרשה להודיע מעלת ארץ ישראל על כל הארצות לחיים ולמתים ועוד לקיים דבר ד' לאברהם להיות לו נחלה:
Ramban the whole verse
Hebrew
וְטַעַם
Rambanfollows וְאַחֲרֵי כֵן֩ קָבַ֨ר אַבְרָהָ֜ם אֶת שָׂרָ֣ה אִשְׁתּ֗וֹ אֶל מְעָרַ֞ת שְׂדֵ֧ה הַמַּכְפֵּלָ֛ה הִ֣וא חֶבְר֑וֹן בְּאֶ֖רֶץ כְּנָֽעַן׃
Ramban: 'in the land of Canaan' is written to show that the place is in the land of Canaan, in the mountain where the Canaanite dwells, and not in the land of the Philistines, where Abraham had lived many days (21:34). He says the Hittites are of the families of Canaan. He gives homiletic reasons for the passage (God's kindness to Abraham, the patriarchs' burial place to be honoured) and says he does not understand the reason of 'Rabbi Abraham' (Ibn Ezra) that it shows the excellence of the land. The English follows his plain point about the land.
Hebrew

Ancient Near East
  • Mamre and Hebron: the verse says 'before Mamre, that is Hebron'. The Torah gives this place more than one name: here Mamre and Hebron, in 23:2 'Kiriath-arba, that is Hebron', and in 35:27 'Mamre, Kiriath-arba, that is Hebron'. Radak takes Mamre as a name of the city. The English gives the names as the verse gives them.
  • Canaan: the land is named as the land of Canaan, west of the Jordan. Ramban's point is that the text names Canaan, not the land of the Philistines, to place this city in the hill country.
Apparatus
  • Ketiv and qere: the consonantal text has הוא ('he') for the feminine pronoun, as everywhere in the Pentateuch; the qere הִיא ('she, it') is read and translated.
  • Radak identifies Mamre and Hebron as one city (see 23:17); the verse itself says 'Mamre, that is Hebron'. Radak and Onkelos read אֶל מְעָרַת as 'in the cave'; the English keeps 'into'.
23:20 · ס

And the field and the cave which was in it were made over to Abraham as a possession for a grave from the Hittites.

and-stood the-field and-the-cave which in-it to-Abraham to-possession-of grave from-with sons-of Heth

Grammar
  • The verse returns to the verb of 23:17, 'and stood', with the field and the cave as the subject. The verb is masculine singular for a compound subject, as in 23:17.
  • לַאֲחֻזַּת קָבֶר is 'as a holding of burial': the lamed marks what the field became ('as, for'). אֲחֻזַּת is the construct and קָבֶר the absolute, in its pausal form.
  • The source is named as 'from the sons of Heth' (מֵאֵת), not as Ephron, who is the seller named in 23:17. The English keeps the Hebrew's source.
  • Accents: etnaḥta on קָ֑בֶר (23:20.8) divides the verse; the silluq on חֵֽת (23:20.11) ends it. The paragraph mark after the verse closes the section of the field.

The English gives the Hebrew's source, 'from the Hittites', as the people, as the Hebrew does.

Radakrecords מֵאֵ֖ת בְּנֵי חֵֽת׃
Radak: Ephron gave it with their consent and will, since it seemed good in the eyes of all of them that Abraham should have a holding among them. This explains 'from' as the people's agreement. It is an account of what happened, so it stays in the note; the English keeps 'from the Hittites'.

24:1

Abraham was old and advanced in years, and the LORD had blessed Abraham in all things.

and-Abraham old came in-days; and-LORD blessed ACC-Abraham in-all

Grammar
  • The clause וְאַבְרָהָם זָקֵן בָּא בַּיָּמִים has a noun subject and a qatal, so it is background to the main clause, which is the blessing.
  • The idiom בָּא בַּיָּמִים, 'come in the days', means advanced in years; the English keeps it as one phrase and gives no age.
  • וַיהוָה בֵּרַךְ אֶת־אַבְרָהָם repeats the background pattern with the divine name as subject; 'had blessed' is that pluperfect.
  • The verse ends with בַּכֹּל, 'in all' (כֹּל with the article and ב); what the blessing consisted of is Ibn Ezra's gloss and stays in the commentary.

The English gives the words only. What the blessing consisted of (length of days, wealth, honour, sons) is Ibn Ezra's gloss and is kept in the commentary. Rashi's numerical reading of בַּכֹּל is a midrash and is recorded, not followed.

Commentary (9)
Rashinot-applicable בֵּרַ֥ךְ אֶת אַבְרָהָ֖ם בַּכֹּֽל׃
Rashi: בַּכֹּל has the numerical value of בֵּן (son, 52), and since Abraham had a son he had to marry him off. A numerical reading and a reason for the errand; it does not bear on the English.

Ibn Ezranormativefollows בֵּרַ֥ךְ אֶת אַבְרָהָ֖ם בַּכֹּֽל׃
Ibn Ezra: 'blessed in all' means in length of days, wealth, honour and sons, which he calls all of man's desire. He adds that the midrash which makes 'Bakkol' the name of a daughter of Abraham would have to add a further ב, a beth of service ('with Bakkol'), which the text lacks. The English 'in all things' takes the preposition and the word as they stand; his list of what the blessing was stays in the note.

לֹא הָיָה יָכוֹל לְהַשִּׂיאָהּ רַק לִבְנֵי כְּנַעַן הָאֲרוּרִים, וְאִם יְשַׁלְּחֶנָּה לְאַרְצוֹ גַּם כֵּן תַּעֲבֹד שָׁם עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה כְּמוֹתָם, כִּי הָאִשָּׁה בִּרְשׁוּת בַּעְלָהּ, וְאַבְרָהָם לֹא יַחְפֹּץ שֶׁיֵּצֵא זַרְעוֹ הַכָּשֵׁר מִשָּׂרָה אִשְׁתּוֹ חוּצָה לָאָרֶץ, וְאַף כִּי יַעֲבֹד עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה. וְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה דָּרַשׁ כִּי בַּת הָיְתָה לוֹ, דַּאֲפִילּוּ בְּרַתָּא לָא חַסְּרֵהּ רַחֲמָנָא (שם קמא), וְהִיא הַבְּרָכָה בַּכֹּל, כִּי הָיָה לוֹ כָּל אֲשֶׁר יַחְמְדוּ הָאֲנָשִׁים, לֹא חָסַר דָּבָר. וּבָאוּ אֲחֵרִים וְהִזְכִּירוּ שֵׁם הַבַּת, וּבֶאֱמֶת שֶׁאֵין הַכַּוָּנָה לַאֲחֵרִים וְהַמַּחְלֹקֶת לָהֶם עִם רַבִּי יְהוּדָה לְהוֹדִיעַ אוֹתָנוּ שֵׁם הַבַּת הַזֹּאת בִּלְבַד, וְחָלִילָה לָהֶם שֶׁיּוֹצִיאוּ בִּרְכָתוֹ שֶׁל אַבְרָהָם שֶׁהִיא גְּדוֹלָה וּכְלָלִית לְעִנְיָן זֶה, שֶׁיֹּאמַר הַכָּתוּב כִּי בֵּרַךְ אֹתוֹ הַשֵּׁם בְּבַת אַחַת שֶׁשְּׁמָהּ כָּךְ, אֲבָל אֲחֵרִים חִדְּשׁוּ בְּפֵרוּשׁ הַכָּתוּב הַזֶּה עִנְיָן עָמֹק מְאֹד, וְדָרְשׁוּ בָּזֶה סוֹד מִסּוֹדוֹת הַתּוֹרָה, וְאָמְרוּ כִּי "בַּכֹּל" תִּרְמֹז עַל עִנְיָן גָּדוֹל, וְהוּא שֶׁיֵּשׁ לְהקב"ה מִדָּה תִּקָּרֵא "כֹּל", מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהִיא יְסוֹד הַכֹּל, וּבָהּ נֶאֱמַר (ישעיהו מד כד) "אָנֹכִי ה' עֹשֶׂה כֹּל", וְהוּא שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (קהלת ה ח) "וְיִתְרוֹן אֶרֶץ בַּכֹּל הוּא", יֹאמַר כִּי יִתְרוֹן הָאָרֶץ וְטוּבָהּ הַגָּדוֹל הַשּׁוֹפֵעַ עַל כָּל בָּאֵי עוֹלָם בַּעֲבוּר כִּי בַּכֹּל הִיא, וְהִיא הַמִּדָּה הַשְּׁמִינִית מי"ג מִדּוֹת, וּמִדָּה אַחֶרֶת תִּקָּרֵא "בַּת", נֶאֱצֶלֶת מִמֶּנָּה, וּבָהּ הוּא מַנְהִיג אֶת הַכֹּל, וְהִיא בֵּית דִּינוֹ שֶׁל הקב"ה הַנִּרְמָז בְּמִלַּת "וַה'" בְּכָל מָקוֹם (ב"ר נא ב), וְהִיא שֶׁנִּקְרֵאת "כַּלָּה" בְּסֵפֶר שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים, בַּעֲבוּר שֶׁהִיא כְּלוּלָה מִן הַכֹּל, וְהִיא שֶׁחֲכָמִים מְכַנִּים שְׁמָהּ "כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל" בִּמְקוֹמוֹת רַבִּים, בַּעֲבוּר שֶׁהִיא כְּנוּסַת הַכֹּל. וְהַמִּדָּה הַזֹּאת הָיְתָה לְאַבְרָהָם כְּבַת, כִּי הוּא אִישׁ הַחֶסֶד וְיִתְנַהֵג בָּזוֹ. וּלְכָךְ אָמְרוּ אֲחֵרִים כִּי אֵין הַבְּרָכָה הַזֹּאת שֶׁנִּתְבָּרֵךְ בַּכֹּל רוֹמֶזֶת עַל שֶׁהוֹלִיד בַּת מִשָּׂרָה אִשְׁתּוֹ אוֹ שֶׁלֹּא הוֹלִיד, אֲבָל הִיא רוֹמֶזֶת עִנְיָן גָּדוֹל, שֶׁבֵּרַךְ אוֹתוֹ בַּמִּדָּה שֶׁהִיא בְּתוֹךְ מִדַּת הַכֹּל, וְלָכֵן תִּקָּרֵא גַּם הִיא "כֹּל", כִּלְשׁוֹן "כִּי שְׁמִי בְּקִרְבּוֹ" (שמות כג כא), וְהִנֵּה הוּא מְבֹרָךְ בַּשָּׁמַיִם וּבָאָרֶץ, וּלְכָךְ אָמַר "בַּה' אֱלֹהֵי הַשָּׁמַיִם וֵאלֹהֵי הָאָרֶץ". וְהָעִנְיָן הַזֶּה נִמְצָא לְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ רָמוּז בַּהַגָּדוֹת בִּמְקוֹמוֹת רַבִּים, כְּעִנְיָן שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּמִדְרַשׁ חָזִיתָ (שיר השירים ג כא), שָׁאַל רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַאי אֶת רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי, אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתָּ מֵאָבִיךָ מַהוּ "בָּעֲטָרָה שֶׁעִטְּרָה לוֹ אִמּוֹ" (שיר השירים ג יא), אָמַר לוֹ הֵן, אָמַר לוֹ הֵיאַךְ, אָמַר לוֹ מָשָׁל לְמֶלֶךְ שֶׁהָיְתָה לוֹ בַּת יְחִידָה וְהָיָה מְחַבְּבָה יוֹתֵר מִדַּאי וְהָיָה קוֹרֵא אוֹתָהּ בִּתִּי, לֹא זָז מֵחַבְּבָהּ עַד שֶׁקָּרָא אוֹתָהּ אֲחוֹתִי, וְלֹא זָז מֵחַבְּבָהּ עַד שֶׁקָּרָא אוֹתָהּ אִמִּי, כָּךְ בַּתְּחִלָּה חִבֵּב הקב"ה אֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל וּקְרָאָן בִּתִּי, הֲדָא הוּא דִכְתִיב (תהלים מה יא) "שִׁמְעִי בַת וּרְאִי", וְלֹא זָז מֵחַבְּבָן עַד שֶׁקְּרָאָן אֲחוֹתִי, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (שיר השירים ה ב) "פִּתְחִי לִי אֲחֹתִי רַעְיָתִי", וְלֹא זָז מֵחַבְּבָן עַד שֶׁקְּרָאָן אִמִּי, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (ישעיהו נא ד) "הַקְשִׁיבוּ אֵלַי עַמִּי וּלְאוּמִּי", לְאִמִּי כְּתִיב, עָמַד רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַאי וּנְשָׁקוֹ עַל רֹאשׁוֹ, אָמַר לוֹ אִלּוּ לֹא בָּאתִי אֶלָּא לִשְׁמֹעַ זֶה הַדָּבָר מִפִּיךְ דַּי. וּמְבֹאָר זֶה בְּמִדְרָשׁוֹ שֶׁל ר' נְחוּנְיָא בֶּן הַקָּנָה (ספר הבהיר כב), אָמְרוּ בַּפָּסוּק "אָנֹכִי ה' עֹשֶׂה כֹּל נֹטֶה שָׁמַיִם לְבַדִּי רֹקַע הָאָרֶץ מֵאִתִּי" (ישעיהו מד כד), אֲנִי כְּשֶׁנָּטַעְתִּי אִילָן זֶה לְהִשְׁתַּעֲשֵׁעַ בּוֹ כָּל הָעוֹלָם וְרָקַעְתִּי בּוֹ הַכֹּל, וְקָרָאתִי שְׁמוֹ כֹּל, שֶׁהַכֹּל תָּלוּי בּוֹ וְהַכֹּל מִמֶּנּוּ יֹצֵא וְהַכֹּל צְרִיכִין לוֹ, וּבוֹ צוֹפִין וְלוֹ מְחַכִּים, וּמִשָּׁם פּוֹרְחִים נְשָׁמוֹת, לְבַדִּי הָיִיתִי כְּשֶׁעָשִׂיתִי אוֹתוֹ, וְלֹא יִגְדַּל עָלָיו מַלְאָךְ לֵאמֹר אֲנִי קָדַמְתִּי לְךָ, גַּם בְּעֵת שֶׁרָקַעְתִּי אַרְצִי שֶׁבָּהּ נָטַעְתִּי וְשֵׁרַשְׁתִּי אִילָן זֶה, וְשִׂמַּחְתִּים בְּיַחַד וְשָׂמַחְתִּי בָהֶם, מִי אִתִּי, שֶׁגִּלִּיתִי לוֹ סוֹדִי זֶה, עַד כָּאן. וְעוֹד שָׁם מְבֹאָר מַאי "בְּרֹגֶז רַחֵם תִּזְכֹּר" (חבקוק ג ב), אָמַר בְּעֵת שֶׁחָטְאוּ לְךָ בָּנֶיךָ וְתִכְעַס עֲלֵיהֶם, רַחֵם תִּזְכֹּר, וּמַאי "רַחֵם תִּזְכֹּר", זְכֹר אוֹתוֹ שֶׁאָמַר "אֶרְחָמְךָ ה' חִזְקִי" (תהלים יח ב) וְנָתַתָּ לוֹ הַמִּדָּה הַזֹּאת שֶׁהִיא שְׁכִינָתָן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל, וּזְכֹר בְּנוֹ שֶׁיְּרָשָׁהּ וְנָתַתָּ לוֹ הַמִּדָּה הַזֹּאת שֶׁהִיא שְׁכִינָתוֹ שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל, דִּכְתִיב (מלכים א ה כו) "וַה' נָתַן חָכְמָה לִשְׁלֹמֹה", וּזְכֹר אֲבִיהֶם אַבְרָהָם, דִּכְתִיב "זֶרַע אַבְרָהָם אוֹהֲבִי" (ישעיהו מא ח), וּ"בְקֶרֶב שָׁנִים תּוֹדִיעַ" (חבקוק ג ב). וּמֵהֵיכָן הָיְתָה בַּת לְאַבְרָהָם, הֵן, דִּכְתִיב "וַה' בֵּרַךְ אֶת אַבְרָהָם בַּכֹּל", וּכְתִיב (ישעיהו מג ז) "כֹּל הַנִּקְרָא בִשְׁמִי וְלִכְבוֹדִי בְּרָאתִיו", הַהִיא בְּרָכָה הָיְתָה בִּתּוֹ, אוֹ לֹא הָיְתָה אֶלָּא אִמּוֹ, הֵן, בִּתּוֹ הָיְתָה, מָשָׁל לְאָדוֹן שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ עֶבֶד שָׁלֵם תָּמִים לְפָנָיו וְנִסָּהוּ בְּכַמָּה נִסְיוֹנוֹת וְעָמַד בְּכֻלָּן, אָמַר הָאָדוֹן מָה אֶתֵּן לְעֶבֶד זֶה אוֹ מַה אֶעֱשֶׂה לוֹ, אֶלָּא אֲצַוֶּנּוּ לְאָחִי הַגָּדוֹל לְיַעֲצוֹ וּלְשָׁמְרוֹ וּלְכַבְּדוֹ. חָזַר הָעֶבֶד עִם אָחִיו הַגָּדוֹל וְלָמַד מִדּוֹתָיו, אֲהָבוֹ הָאָח וּקְרָאוֹ אוֹהֲבִי, דִּכְתִיב "זֶרַע אַבְרָהָם אֹהֲבִי", אָמַר מָה אֶתֵּן לוֹ אוֹ מָה אֶעֱשֶׂה לוֹ, הִנֵּה כְּלִי נָאֶה עָשִׂיתִי וּבוֹ מַרְגָּלִיּוֹת נָאוֹת וְאֵין כְּמוֹתָן, וְהֵם סְגֻלַּת מְלָכִים, אֶתְּנֶנָּה לוֹ וְיִזְכֶּה בִּמְקוֹמִי. הֲדָא הוּא דִכְתִיב "וַה' בֵּרַךְ אֶת אַבְרָהָם בַּכֹּל", עַד כָּאן. וְאִם תָּבִין מָה שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי תֵּדַע מַאֲמַר הַנָּשִׁים הָאֲרוּרוֹת שֶׁאָמְרוּ "וּמִן אָז חָדַלְנוּ לְקַטֵּר לִמְלֶכֶת הַשָּׁמַיִם חָסַרְנוּ כֹל" (ירמיהו מד יח), וְלָמָּה נִכְתְּבָה הַמִּלָּה חַסְרַת הָאָלֶ"ף, וְתַשְׁכִּיל דְּבָרִים רַבִּים סְתוּמִים בַּתּוֹרָה וּמִקְרָא. וְאִלּוּ יָדַע זֶה הַמִּתְהַדֵּר בְּסוֹדוֹתָיו תֵּאָלַמְנָה שְׂפָתָיו מֵהַלְעִיג עַל דִּבְרֵי רַבּוֹתֵינוּ. וְלָכֵן כָּתַבְתִּי זֶה לִסְכֹּר פִּי הַדּוֹבְרִים עַל הַצַּדִּיקִים עָתָק:
Radak וְאַבְרָהָ֣ם זָקֵ֔ן
Hebrew
פֹּעַל עָבָר אוֹ תֹּאַר.
Radak בָּ֖א בַּיָּמִ֑ים
Hebrew
בַּיָּמִים שֶׁהֵם הַשְׁלָמַת יְמֵי אָדָם בָּעוֹלָם, וְרָצָה לְהַשִּׂיא אִשָּׁה לִבְנוֹ יִצְחָק בְּחַיָּיו.

24:2

Abraham said to his servant, the elder of his household, who ruled over all that he had, "Put your hand under my thigh, please,

and-said Abraham to his-servant elder-of his-household the-ruling over-all that to-him; put pray your-hand under my-thigh

Grammar
  • The main clause is a wayyiqtol, 'and said'; the speech follows it directly with no second introduction until the servant speaks in 24:5.
  • שִׂים נָא יָדְךָ תַּחַת יְרֵכִי is an imperative with the particle נָא, 'please'; the object is the hand, and its place is given by תַּחַת.
  • The servant is described by a construct chain, 'the elder of his household', and one participle with its object, 'who ruled over all that he had'; the English keeps that order.
  • The gesture itself is the thing to be read: the hand is placed under the thigh of the one who speaks. The meanings given to it are the commentators' and are kept out of the English.

The gesture is described plainly. Three readings are recorded: an oath gesture, a sign of being under another's authority, and an allusion to circumcision. Ibn Ezra's choice is not adopted in the English because his explanation is what the gesture meant, which the English does not state.

Ibn Ezranormativerecords שִֽׂים נָ֥א יָדְךָ֖ תַּ֥חַת יְרֵכִֽי׃
Ibn Ezra: some say the gesture alludes to circumcision; he answers that then the man would have sworn by the covenant of circumcision and not by the Name. His own view is that in those days it was the custom for a man to put his hand under the thigh of the one whose authority he was under: 'if you are under my authority, put your hand under my thigh'. The master sits with his thigh over the hand, as in 'here my hand is under your authority, to do your will'. He adds that the custom still exists in the land of Hodu. The English states the gesture only.

Ancient Near East
  • The hand under the thigh (24:2) is a gesture with a plain description: the servant is to put his hand under Abraham's thigh, the thigh of the one who speaks. The same gesture is made by Joseph for Jacob before a promise about Jacob's burial (47:29). The meaning is not stated and is read variously. Ibn Ezra takes it as a sign that the one who places his hand is under the authority of the other, and Radak as a custom for confirming a charge; Rashi takes it as an allusion to circumcision, as the hand rests on something holy. Some also link it to the fact that descendants are said to 'come out of the thigh' (46:26), taking the thigh as the seat of procreation; that is a suggestion, not settled. The text does not choose among these, and the English does not choose.
Apparatus
  • 24:2: the gesture is read three ways in the commentary (oath, subjection, circumcision); the English line gives only 'put your hand under my thigh'.
24:3

and I will make you swear by the LORD, God of heaven and God of earth, that you shall not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites among whom I dwell,

and-I-will-make-you-swear by-LORD God-of heavens and-God-of earth; that not you-will-take wife for-my-son from-daughters-of the-Canaanite; that I dwell in-its-midst

Grammar
  • The oath is a hifil with a 1st-person subject: 'I will make you swear'. The content of the oath follows in the relative clause אֲשֶׁר לֹא־תִקַּח.
  • The relative clause is the object of the oath, not a clause about the daughters: 'that you shall not take a wife'.
  • The epithet is a construct plural, 'God of the heavens and God of the earth'; both parts are kept in the English.
  • הַכְּנַעֲנִי is singular with the article but collective; the English uses the plural 'Canaanites' for the group.

The English keeps the two-part epithet of the oath and the collective Canaanite. The reasons Ibn Ezra gives for the epithet are not part of the English.

Ibn Ezranormativenot-applicable the whole verse
Ibn Ezra explains the two epithets here: the match of a daughter to a man on earth is made from heaven, and he says this is a secret. It is a reason for the epithets, not a reading of their words.

Grammar
  • כִּי at the start of the verse turns the negative of 24:3 into a positive command: 'but rather to my country you shall go'.
  • The two verbs of the command are an imperfect (תֵּלֵךְ) and a perfect with vav (וְלָקַחְתָּ) that continues it.
  • לִבְנִי לְיִצְחָק gives the son twice, with ל and then the name; the English makes this 'my son Isaac'.
  • The speech of Abraham that opened in 24:2 closes here.

'Birthplace' takes the place sense of מוֹלֶדֶת that Ibn Ezra, Radak and Rashi give. The kindred sense of the word is in the lexicon entry and is not used in the English.

  • 'My country' and 'my birthplace' (24:4, 24:7): Ibn Ezra and Rashi name Haran as the place where Abraham's family settled and Ur of the Chaldeans as the birthplace, though Radak takes 'my country' to be Aram-naharaim. 24:5

The servant said to him, "Perhaps the woman will not be willing to follow me to this land. Shall I indeed bring back your son to the land from which you came?"

and-said to-him the-servant; perhaps not will-be-willing the-woman; to-go after-me to the-land this; bring-back I-will-bring-back; ACC; your-son to the-land; that you-went-out from-there

Grammar
  • The servant's speech is two questions: a doubt, 'perhaps the woman will not be willing', and a question, 'shall I bring your son back?'
  • הֶהָשֵׁב אָשִׁיב is an infinitive absolute before a finite form of the same root: an emphatic question that the English states once.
  • The same noun, 'the land', is used twice: once with the demonstrative 'this', once with a relative clause 'from which you came'.
  • The servant speaks of Abraham's son by the suffix 'your son', and of the woman as the object of 'follow me'.

The English gives 'shall I indeed bring back' for the emphatic question: 'indeed' carries the infinitive absolute. Ibn Ezra's comment on the pointing of the he is not a reading of the words and is kept in the commentary.

24:6

Abraham said to him, "Take heed to yourself, lest you bring back my son there.

and-said to-him Abraham; take-heed to-you; lest you-will-bring-back; ACC; my-son there

Grammar
  • הִשָּׁמֶר לְךָ is a nifal imperative with a dative suffix: 'take heed to yourself'.
  • פֶּן with the imperfect gives the result Abraham fears: 'lest you bring back my son there'.
  • Abraham's answer is one speech that opens here and runs to the end of 24:8.

The English keeps the servant as 'you' throughout. The root is שׁמר, 'keep'; the nifal sense 'be on your guard' is the one the warning requires. Ibn Ezra's rule on the stress of הִשָּׁמֶר puts this form, stressed on the penult, under שְׁמִירָה, so it agrees with the English.

Commentary (4)
Ibn Ezranormativefollows the whole verse
Ibn Ezra: every הִשָּׁמֶר stressed on the penultimate syllable comes from שְׁמִירָה (keeping); one stressed on the last comes from שְׁמָרִים (lees, dregs), as in 'be still and quiet' (Isaiah 7:4), like 'he is at ease on his lees' (Jeremiah 48:11). The form here has its accent on the shin, the penultimate syllable, so by his own rule it is from שׁמר 'keep', and the English 'take heed' agrees.

וַאֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבְרָהָם אִסְתַּמַּר לָךְ דִּילְמָא תָתֵיב יָת בְּרִי לְתַמָּן:
24:7

The LORD, God of heaven, who took me from my father's house and from the land of my birth, and who spoke to me and who swore to me, saying, 'To your offspring I will give this land'; may he send his angel before you, and you shall take a wife for my son from there.

the-LORD God-of heavens; who took-me from-house-of my-father and-from-land-of my-birth; and-who spoke to-me; and-who swore to-me; saying to-your-offspring I-will-give; ACC; the-land this; he will-send his-angel before-you; and-you-will-take wife for-my-son from-there

Grammar
  • Three relative clauses, each with אֲשֶׁר, hang from 'the LORD, God of heaven': who took me, who spoke to me, who swore to me. The main clause begins with 'he will send'.
  • לֵאמֹר לְזַרְעֲךָ אֶתֵּן אֶת־הָאָרֶץ הַזֹּאת is speech inside Abraham's speech, so it is in single quotes.
  • The yiqtol הוּא יִשְׁלַח is read as a wish, 'may he send'; the next verse's 'if the woman will not be willing' supports Ibn Ezra's reading (see commentary).
  • The weqatal וְלָקַחְתָּ continues the purpose of the sending: 'and you shall take a wife'.

The epithet 'God of heaven' stands alone here, unlike 24:3, where 'and God of earth' is added. Rashi explains the difference; the English keeps the words as they stand. The yiqtol הוּא יִשְׁלַח can be read as a plain future, 'he will send his angel', or as a wish, 'may he send his angel'. The English takes the wish with Ibn Ezra (a prayer, since the woman may refuse in 24:8) and Sforno; the plain future is the other reading and is recorded in the context.

Rashi explains why the epithet here is 'God of heaven' alone: when God took Abraham from his father's house he was 'God of heaven and not God of earth', because the people of the world did not know him and his name was not common in the land. A reason for the wording, not a reading of its grammar.

לְשׁוֹן רַשִׁ"י (רש"י על בראשית כ"ד:ז'), מִבֵּית אָבִי מֵחָרָן, וּמֵאֶרֶץ מוֹלַדְתִּי מֵאוּר כַּשְׂדִּים. אִם כֵּן "אֶל אַרְצִי וְאֶל מוֹלַדְתִּי תֵּלֵךְ" יִהְיֶה אוּר כַּשְׂדִּים, וְחָלִילָה חָלִילָה שֶׁיִּתְעָרֵב זֶרַע הַקֹּדֶשׁ בִּבְנֵי חָם הַפּוֹשֵׁעַ. אוּלַי יֹאמַר שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ מִשְׁפָּחָה שָׁם מִזַּרְעוֹ שֶׁל שֵׁם, אֲבָל הָעֶבֶד לְחָרָן הָלַךְ כַּאֲשֶׁר דִּבֵּר אֲדֹנָיו. וְאוּלַי יַחְשֹׁב הָרַב כִּי אֶרֶץ מוֹלַדְתּוֹ אוּר כַּשְׂדִּים, אֲבָל "מוֹלַדְתִּי" הִיא מִשְׁפַּחְתִּי, וְ"אַרְצִי" אֶרֶץ אֲשֶׁר גָּר בָּהּ. וְכָל אֵלֶּה דְּבָרִים בְּטֵלִים, כִּי בְּכָאן אָמַר "וְלָקַחְתָּ אִשָּׁה לִבְנִי מִשָּׁם", וְעוֹד כִּי יָמִים רַבִּים עָמַד בְּאֶרֶץ כְּנַעַן יוֹתֵר מֵחָרָן, וְלָמָּה תִּקָּרֵא חָרָן אַרְצוֹ בַּעֲבוּר שֶׁגָּר בָּהּ יָמִים. אֲבָל "אֶל אַרְצִי וְאֶל מוֹלַדְתִּי", אַרְצִי שֶׁשָּׁם מוֹלַדְתִּי, כִּי שָׁם עָמַד וּמִשָּׁם הָיוּ אֲבוֹתָיו מֵעוֹלָם, וּכְבָר נִתְבָּאֵר (לעיל יא כח יב א). וּבִבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה (בראשית רבה נ"ט:י'), מִבֵּית אָבִי זוֹ בֵּיתוֹ שֶׁל אָבִיו, וּמֵאֶרֶץ מוֹלַדְתִּי זוֹ שְׁכוּנָתִי. וְיִתָּכֵן שֶׁיִּהְיֶה טַעַם "אֶל אַרְצִי וְאֶל מוֹלַדְתִּי" אַרְצִי וּמִשְׁפַּחְתִּי, כִּי גַּם בְּאַנְשֵׁי אַרְצוֹ לֹא יַחְפֹּץ רַק בְּמִשְׁפַּחְתּוֹ, וְכֵן "וְלָקַחְתָּ אִשָּׁה לִבְנִי מִשָּׁם" רֶמֶז אֶל "מִבֵּית אָבִי", וְכֵן יֹאמַר הָעֶבֶד (בראשית כ"ד:מ') "וְלָקַחְתָּ אִשָּׁה לִבְנִי מִמִּשְׁפַּחְתִּי וּמִבֵּית אָבִי", וְאָמַר (שם מא) "כִּי תָבֹא אֶל מִשְׁפַּחְתִּי", אוֹ שֶׁהָיָה הָעֶבֶד אוֹמֵר כֵּן לְכַבְּדָם שֶׁיִּשְׁמְעוּ לוֹ:

Other readings (1)
  • ה֗וּא יִשְׁלַ֤ח מַלְאָכוֹ֙ לְפָנֶ֔יךָ: he will send his angel before you plain future The yiqtol read as a plain future: a promise, not a wish. The English follows Ibn Ezra and Sforno, who read a prayer ('may he send').
Ancient Near East
  • 'My father's house' and 'the land of my birth' (24:7): Rashi names Haran and Ur of the Chaldeans; the text of this unit names neither.
  • 'May he send his angel' (24:7): the verb is a yiqtol, which allows a plain future ('he will send his angel') or a wish. Ibn Ezra takes it as a prayer, because Abraham goes on to allow that the woman may be unwilling (24:8); Sforno also reads a wish. The plain future is the other reading; Abraham uses the same words when he tells the servant's story in 24:40.
Apparatus
  • 24:7.1: the epithet is 'God of heaven' without 'and God of earth' as in 24:3; the commentators' explanations are in the commentary.
24:8

If the woman will not be willing to follow you, then you shall be clear of this oath of mine; only my son you shall not bring back there."

and-if not she-will-be-willing the-woman to-go after-you; and-you-shall-be-clear from-my-oath this; only ACC my-son; not you-shall-bring-back there

Grammar
  • The conditional has a protasis (8.1 to 8.6), 'if the woman will not be willing', and an apodosis (8.7) introduced by the vav of נִקִּיתָ: 'then you shall be clear'.
  • נִקִּיתָ is a nifal perfect of a III-he verb: the pattern is regular, and the English 'shall be clear' gives the nifal sense of freedom from an obligation.
  • The last clause puts the object first: רַק אֶת־בְּנִי לֹא תָשֵׁב שָׁמָּה, 'only my son you shall not bring back there'. The restriction applies to the son alone.
  • The speech closes here, at the end of the unit's last verse.

The English gives the plain sense of the hifil: the servant is not to bring the son back. Ibn Ezra's remark (that Isaac is to stay in the land of Israel, for Abraham's sake) states what the prohibition secures and is recorded in the commentary. Rashi's reading of the release (a wife from the daughters of Aner, Eshkol and Mamre) is recorded and not followed.

Commentary (6)
Rashideclines וְנִקִּ֕יתָ מִשְּׁבֻעָתִ֖י
Rashi reads the release from the oath as permission to take a wife for Isaac from the daughters of Aner, Eshkol and Mamre. The Hebrew here names no family; the English keeps 'be clear of this oath'.

Rashinot-applicable רַ֣ק אֶת בְּנִ֔י

לֹא הִרְשָׁה אוֹתוֹ לָקַחַת לוֹ אִשָּׁה מִבְּנוֹת כְּנַעַן, אֲבָל שֶׁיִּהְיֶה הוּא פָּטוּר וַה' הַטּוֹב בְּעֵינָיו יַעֲשֶׂה. וְרַשִׁ"י כָּתַב (רש"י על בראשית כ"ד:ח') וְקַח לוֹ אִשָּׁה מִבְּנוֹת עָנֵר אֶשְׁכּוֹל וּמַמְרֵא. וְאִם כְּנַעֲנִים הֵם, חָלִילָה לוֹ. וּבֶאֱמֶת שֶׁהֵם מִזֶּרַע כְּנַעַן, שֶׁהַכָּתוּב אוֹמֵר (בראשית י"ד:י"ג) "מַמְרֵא הָאֱמֹרִי אֲחִי אֶשְׁכֹּל וַאֲחִי עָנֵר", וּבִבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה (בראשית רבה נ"ט:ח') אָמְרוּ "אֲשֶׁר לֹא תִקַּח אִשָּׁה" וְגוֹ', הִזְהִירוֹ בִּבְנוֹת כְּנַעַן עָנֵר אֶשְׁכּוֹל וּמַמְרֵא, כִּי עֲלֵיהֶם אָמַר "אֲשֶׁר אָנֹכִי יוֹשֵׁב בְּקִרְבּוֹ", כִּי הוּא לֹא הָיָה יוֹשֵׁב בְּכָל הַכְּנַעֲנִי כִּי עַמִּים רַבִּים הָיוּ, אֲבָל הִזְהִיר עַל אֵלֶּה בַּעֲלֵי בְּרִיתוֹ וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן עַל הָאֲחֵרִים. אֲבָל "וְנִקִּיתָ מִשְּׁבוּעָתִי", שֶׁיִּהְיֶה הוּא פָּטוּר, וְאַבְרָהָם הוּא הַיּוֹדֵעַ בְּיִצְחָק הַצַּדִּיק שֶׁיִּשְׁמַע לְאָבִיו וְשֶׁיִּזָּהֵר בָּהֶם, וְיֵלֵךְ לוֹ אֶל יִשְׁמָעֵאל אוֹ לְלוֹט וְיֶתֶר הָעַמִּים. וְיִתָּכֵן כִּי "מִשְּׁבוּעָתִי זֹאת" רֶמֶז לְמָה שֶׁאָמַר "וְלָקַחְתָּ אִשָּׁה לִבְנִי מִשָּׁם", כִּי אוּלַי הָיְתָה הַשְּׁבוּעָה עַל הַכֹּל, וְלֹא יִרְמֹז לַאֲשֶׁר אָמַר לוֹ "לֹא תִקַּח אִשָּׁה לִבְנִי מִבְּנוֹת הַכְּנַעֲנִי", וְזֶה טַעַם "זֹאת", וּלְכָךְ אָמַר הָעֶבֶד "וְאֶפְנֶה עַל יָמִין אוֹ עַל שְׂמֹאל" (בראשית כ"ד:מ"ט), וְלֹא אָמַר "אָשׁוּבָה לִי":

24:9

And the servant put his hand under the thigh of Abraham his master, and he swore to him concerning this matter.

and-put the-servant the-object-marker his-hand under thigh-of Abraham his-master and-swore to-him on the-matter this

Grammar
  • Two wayyiqtol verbs carry the sentence: וַיָּשֶׂם (he put) and וַיִּשָּׁבַע (and he swore). The servant is the subject of the first; the second has the same subject in the verb.
  • The nifal וַיִּשָּׁבַע is the form of an oath: the one who swears is the subject, the person sworn to takes לוֹ 'to him', and the matter takes עַל 'concerning'.
  • The etnaḥta on אֲדֹנָיו (24:9.8) divides the verse after 'his master'; the silluq on הַזֶּה ends it.
  • אֲדֹנָיו is a plural construct form with a singular sense ('his master'). The English reads it as singular.

The English keeps the object 'his hand' and the place 'under the thigh' as the Hebrew gives them, with no explanation of the gesture.

Commentary (3)
Radaknot-applicable וַיָּ֤שֶׂם
Radak's note on the first verb is a one-word gloss (מְבֹאָר, 'explained'). It does not bear on the English.
Hebrew
מְבֹאָר.
Targum Onkelosrecords the whole verse
Onkelos renders the oath with the Aramaic וְקַיֵּם לֵיהּ, 'confirmed to him', concerning this word. The English keeps 'swore', the Hebrew verb of an oath.
Hebrew
וְשַׁוִּי עַבְדָא יָת יְדֵיהּ תְּחוֹת יַרְכָא דְאַבְרָהָם רִבּוֹנֵיהּ וְקַיֵּם לֵיהּ עַל פִּתְגָּמָא הָדֵין:
Sfornorecords וַיִּשָּׁ֣בַֽע ל֔וֹ עַל הַדָּבָ֖ר הַזֶּֽה׃
Sforno: he swore 'with all the conditions that Abraham said to him' (נִשְׁבַּע עִם כָּל הַתְּנָאִים), so 'this matter' names the conditions. The English keeps 'concerning this matter', which does not say what the matter was.
Hebrew
נִשְׁבַּע עִם כָּל הַתְּנָאִים שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ אַבְרָהָם:
Ancient Near East
  • The oath gesture: the hand is put under the thigh (יָרֵךְ) of the one to whom the oath is sworn. Scholars differ on its meaning. Some take the thigh as the seat of descent, so that the oath is sworn on the master's offspring; others see a conventional sign of an oath. The text does not say which, and the English does not choose.
24:10

And the servant took ten camels from his master's camels and went, and all the goods of his master in his hand, and he arose and went to Aram-naharaim, to the city of Nahor.

and-took the-servant ten camels from-camels-of his-master and-went and-all-of goods his-master in-his-hand and-arose and-went to Aram-naharaim to the-city-of Nahor

Grammar
  • Four wayyiqtol verbs move the narrative: וַיִּקַּח (took), וַיֵּלֶךְ (went), וַיָּקׇם (arose), וַיֵּלֶךְ (went).
  • וְכׇל־טוּב אֲדֹנָיו בְּיָדוֹ has no verb. The English keeps it verbless, so that the reader sees the open question of whether the goods are the object of 'took' or a separate clause.
  • מִגְּמַלֵּי אֲדֹנָיו is partitive: ten of the camels of his master, with מִ 'from' before the construct plural.
  • The etnaḥta on בְּיָדוֹ (24:10.11) closes the first part of the verse; the silluq on נָחוֹר (24:10.19) ends it.

The clause 'and all the goods of his master in his hand' is kept verbless. Ramban reads the goods as the object of 'took' (the cargo of the ten camels); Rashi and Radak read a deed of gift. The English does not settle it.

Commentary (12)
Rashinot-applicable מִגְּמַלֵּ֤י אֲדֹנָיו֙
Rashi, from Bereshit Rabbah: the master's camels were marked out, sent out muzzled so that they would not graze in other fields. A homily about the camels; the English does not take it up.

נִכָּרִין הָיוּ מִשְּׁאָר גְּמַלִּים, שֶׁהָיוּ יוֹצְאִין זְמוּמִין מִפְּנֵי הַגֶּזֶל, שֶׁלֹּא יִרְעוּ בִשְׂדוֹת אֲחֵרִים (בראשית רבה):

Ancient Near East
  • Camels: the verse has ten of the master's camels, set out with goods. Whether camels were domesticated and in use as baggage animals in the time of the patriarchs is disputed among scholars. The English says 'camels' and does not settle the question; sense 2 (beasts of burden) is the reading the verse suggests.
  • Aram-naharaim: the verse does not name the two rivers. Rashi and Radak take the name, 'Aram of the two rivers', to describe a region lying between or across two rivers; Onkelos reads 'Aram which is on the Euphrates'. The English keeps the name.
  • The city of Nahor: the verse names no town. Radak identifies it with Ur of the Chaldeans. The English leaves the identification open.
24:11

And he made the camels kneel outside the city by the well of water at evening, at the time of the going out of the women who draw.

and-made-kneel the-camels from-outside to-the-city to the-well-of the-water to-time-of evening to-time-of going-out-of the-women drawing

Grammar
  • וַיַּבְרֵךְ is a hifil wayyiqtol of בָּרַךְ. The binyan gives the causative sense 'made to kneel'; the English does not say 'blessed'.
  • Three prepositional phrases stand in a row: outside the city, by the well of water, and the time, which is given twice (לְעֵת), the second governing the infinitive construct צֵאת.
  • הַשֹּׁאֲבֹת is a feminine plural participle with the article. The verse does not name the water; 'draw' is the English.
  • The darga on וַיַּבְרֵךְ (24:11.1) and the etnaḥta on הַמָּיִם (24:11.7) divide the verse.

Rashifollows וַיַּבְרֵ֧ךְ הַגְּמַלִּ֛ים

24:12

And he said, "LORD, God of my master Abraham, please make it happen before me today, and show kindness to my master Abraham.

and-said LORD God-of my-master Abraham make-it-happen please before-me the-day and-do kindness with my-master Abraham

Grammar
  • The speech is a prayer addressed to God in the second person, with no 'O' before the divine name. Its verb is the wayyiqtol וַיֹּאמַר.
  • The imperatives הַקְרֵה (24:12.6) and וַעֲשֵׂה (24:12.10) are requests; נָא 'please' is set on the first.
  • יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֵי אֲדֹנִי אַבְרָהָם: the divine name, then the construct 'God of my master Abraham'. The first person 'my' is the servant's.
  • The shalshelet on וַיֹּאמַר (24:12.1) is a rare accent that sets this verb apart; it does not itself mark a speech. The etnaḥta on הַיּוֹם (24:12.9) divides the verse after 'today'.
Commentary (4)
Ibn Ezranormativefollows הַקְרֵה נָ֥א לְפָנַ֖י
Ibn Ezra: הַקְרֵה has the sense of "prepare" as in "prepare my desire before me" (הכן הפצי לפני), and he cites "for the LORD your God caused it to meet me" (כִּי הִקְרָה ה' אֱלֹהֶיךָ, 27:20). The English "make it happen before me" takes this: a request that God bring the matter about.

וַאֲמַר יְיָ אֱלָהֵהּ דְּרִבּוֹנִי אַבְרָהָם זַמִּין כְּעַן קֳדָמַי יוֹמָא דֵין וְעִבַד טִיבוּ עִם רִבּוֹנִי אַבְרָהָם:
24:13

Look, I am standing by the spring of water, and the daughters of the men of the city are going out to draw water.

look I standing on spring-of the-waters and-daughters-of men-of the-town going-out to-draw water

Grammar
  • הִנֵּה with the independent pronoun and the participle נִצָּב: 'look, I am standing'. The servant describes his present position.
  • The participle יֹצְאֹת agrees in gender and number with בְּנוֹת: 'going out'. The English 'are going out' supplies the auxiliary.
  • לִשְׁאֹב is a qal infinitive construct: the purpose of going out.
  • The etnaḥta on הַמָּיִם (24:13.6) divides the verse after 'the water'; the silluq on מָיִם (24:13.12) ends it.
Commentary (1)
Targum Onkelosnot-applicable the whole verse
Onkelos's version of the verse follows the same order: the one standing by the spring, the daughters of the men of the town going out to draw water.
Hebrew
הָא אֲנָא קָאֵם עַל עֵינָא דְמַיָּא וּבְנַת אֱנָשֵׁי קַרְתָּא נַפְקַן לְמִמְלֵי מַיָא:
24:14

And it shall be that the girl to whom I say, 'Please tilt your jar, and I will drink,' and she will say, 'Drink, and I will also water your camels,' you have proved her for your servant, for Isaac; and by her I shall know that you have shown kindness to my master."

and-it-shall-be the-girl which I-say to-her tilt-please your-jar and-I-will-drink and-she-will-say drink and-also your-camels I-will-water her you-proved for-your-servant for-Isaac and-by-her I-shall-know that you-did kindness with my-master

Grammar
  • The sign is introduced by a weqatal of הָיָה, 'it shall be' (וְהָיָה), and a relative clause. The speeches in it are imperfects (I say, I will drink, I will water) and a weqatal (וְאָמְרָה, 'and she will say').
  • The verb הֹכַחְתָּ (24:14.16) is a hifil qatal, second person masculine singular: the servant speaks to God. The English takes Ibn Ezra's sense 'prove'.
  • The clause וּבָהּ אֵדַע כִּי עָשִׂיתָ חֶסֶד gives the outcome of the sign: 'by her I shall know that you have shown kindness'. The כִּי is 'that' here.
  • The silluq on אֲדֹנִי (24:14.25) ends the verse.

The sign is a prayer for a particular girl's answer to a test of generosity. The English keeps the verb 'prove' from Ibn Ezra's reading; the other readings of הֹכַחְתָּ and כִּי are in the commentary.

Commentary (13)

Hebrew
רְאוּיָה הִיא לוֹ שֶׁתְּהֵא גּוֹמֶלֶת חֲסָדִים, וּכְדַאי לִכָּנֵס בְּבֵיתוֹ שֶׁל אַבְרָהָם; וּלְשׁוֹן הֹכַחְתָּ בֵּרַרְתָּ, אפרו"בישט בלע"ז:
Rashirecords וּבָ֣הּ אֵדַ֔ע
Rashi reads וּבָהּ אֵדַע as a plea (לְשׁוֹן תְּחִנָּה): 'make me know through her'. The English reads the form as a plain 'I shall know'.
Hebrew
לְשׁוֹן תְּחִנָּה, הוֹדַע לִי בָּהּ:
Rashirecords כִּי עָשִׂ֥יתָ חֶ֖סֶד
Rashi reads כִּי as 'if': 'if she is of his family and fitting for him, I shall know that you did kindness'. The English keeps 'that', the plain sense of כִּי.
Hebrew
אִם תִּהְיֶה מִמִּשְׁפַּחְתּוֹ וְהוֹגֶנֶת לוֹ אֵדַע כִּי עָשִׂית חֶסֶד:
Ibn Ezranormativefollows אֹתָ֤הּ הֹכַ֙חְתָּ֙
Ibn Ezra: the servant relied on the prayer of the prophet (Abraham), which God answered; he was shown in a dream, through the angel, that God's messenger was sent to help him. The servant thought that no one is as generous as his master's family. Ibn Ezra does not know why others are surprised that the servant did not ask in a fitting way, for if another girl had watered him and his camels and then turned out to be of another family, he would have left her and lost nothing; and "whose daughter are you" was already said to her before he gave her anything. The sum: he prayed that God would prove one of his master's family, and the proof she gives is by way of good conduct (דרך מוסר), like a "generous daughter" (בת נדיב); God heard his prayer. The English "you have proved her" follows his sense of הֹכַחְתָּ.

  • The sign is a test set by the servant in prayer: a girl who offers drink to him and to his camels. The verse does not name a custom beyond this, and the English does not add one.
24:15

And it came to pass, before he finished speaking, and look, Rebekah was coming out, who was born to Bethuel son of Milcah, wife of Nahor brother of Abraham, and her jar on her shoulder.

and-it-came-to-pass he before finished to-speak and-look Rebekah coming-out who was-born to-Bethuel son-of Milcah wife-of Nahor brother-of Abraham and-her-jar on her-shoulder

Grammar
  • וַֽיְהִי הוּא טֶרֶם כִּלָּה לְדַבֵּר: 'it came to pass, before he finished speaking'. טֶרֶם takes the qatal and then the infinitive construct.
  • וְהִנֵּה 'and look' introduces the arrival. The participle יֹצֵאת describes Rebekah as coming out at that moment.
  • The relative clause אֲשֶׁר יֻלְּדָה לִבְתוּאֵל uses a pual qatal: 'who was born to Bethuel'.
  • The chain 'son of Milcah, wife of Nahor brother of Abraham' is in the construct: it names Bethuel's mother, then Nahor, whose wife she was. The clause וְכַדָּהּ עַל־שִׁכְמָהּ has no verb.
Commentary (6)
Rambannot-applicable אֲשֶׁ֤ר יֻלְּדָה֙ לִבְתוּאֵ֣ל בֶּן מִלְכָּ֔ה
Ramban explains why the genealogy is given as 'son of Milcah' (the wife, not the concubine Reumah, whose sons Nahor also had), and why the girl names her father's mother first, as girls do (compare 24:28, 'her mother's house'). The English keeps the text's formula.

24:16

And the girl was very good-looking, a virgin, and no man had known her. She went down to the spring, filled her jar, and came up.

and-the-girl good in-appearance very virgin and-man not knew-her and-went-down the-spring and-filled her-jar and-came-up

Grammar
  • טֹבַת מַרְאֶה מְאֹד בְּתוּלָה is a verbless description of the girl: the English supplies 'was' as the copula.
  • לֹא יְדָעָהּ is a negated qatal: 'no man had known her'. The English 'had known' is the past of the completed act.
  • Three wayyiqtols: וַתֵּרֶד 'went down', וַתְּמַלֵּא 'filled', וַתָּעַל 'came up'. The sequence is narrated in order.
  • The ה on הָעַיְנָה is the directional ending, 'to the spring'. The zaqef gadol on בְּתוּלָה (24:16.5) and the silluq on וַתָּעַל (24:16.13) mark the clause and the verse.
Commentary (8)
Rashinot-applicable בְּתוּלָ֕ה
Rashi glosses בְּתוּלָה as 'from the place of virginity' (מִמְּקוֹם בְּתוּלִים), quoting Bereshit Rabbah. The English keeps 'a virgin'.
Hebrew
מִמְּקוֹם בְּתוּלִים (בראשית רבה):
Rashirecords וְאִ֖ישׁ לֹ֣א יְדָעָ֑הּ
Rashi: 'and no man had known her' means she was not as the custom of the women of the nations, who guarded their virginity in one place and gave themselves elsewhere; the verse testifies that she was pure. The English does not adopt the contrast with custom.
